title: Fabricated references in AI-first-authored research: a manually verified audit of all Agents4Science 2025 submissions

decisions.rationale: This is a structurally complete empirical paper. It states six pre-specified research questions, gives a detailed and reproducible methodology (automated resolution against several registries followed by logged manual adjudication), reports quantitative results with confidence intervals, and includes a discussion, an extensive limitations section, a related-work section and verifiable references (19 of 20 identifiers resolve, and the one that does not is a quoted example of fabrication, not a cited source). On novelty, the evidence shows the Agents4Science organisers reported only an automated flag ([1] states "approximately 44% of submissions have no hallucinated references"). Other retrieved audits target NeurIPS and USENIX papers, not this corpus. Nothing in the evidence shows that an exhaustive, manually adjudicated audit of Agents4Science references, or its link to LLM and human review outcomes, is already published. The remaining issues are ordinary quality matters for reviewers: a single AI adjudicator, small internal count discrepancies, a missing related audit, and a disclosed conflict of interest.
key_concerns: Reference check: doi:10.1177/01655515241234567 is 'not_found'. In context the paper quotes it as a placeholder-pattern identifier taken from an audited submission, not as its own source, so it is consistent with the claim. It should still be explicitly marked as a non-resolving example so readers do not take it for a citation.

Reference check: arXiv:2502.01234 and arXiv:2401.12345, also quoted as placeholder-pattern identifiers from submissions, resolve to unrelated works. The registry titles are 'Homeomorphism of the Revuz correspondence for finite energy integrals' and 'Distributionally Robust Receive Combining'. This matches the paper's statement that such identifiers 'resolve to an unrelated work', but the text should say which identifier does which.

Possible citation-title drift: the paper cites Rao and Callison-Burch as 'BibTeX citation errors in scientific publishing agents'. The registry title matches this, but the fetched PDF at the EVIDENCE URL is titled 'BibTeX Citation Hallucinations in Scientific Publishing Agents: Evaluation and Mitigation', suggesting a version change the authors should reconcile.

Adjudication was performed by a single AI agent with no second coder and no inter-rater reliability estimate. The EXISTS versus EXISTS_CORRUPTED boundary involves judgement and drives about 43% of the fabricated count.

Internal count inconsistency in Q5 (Section 5.6): LLM reviews contain explicit statements in 8 affected submissions, 5 of them independent findings, yet 'in the other four' the reviewer echoes the authors' disclosure. The categories need to be reconciled.

Section 5.6 also says explicit statements occurred in 5 clean submissions, 'one by GPT-5 and three by Gemini among them', leaving one unattributed. It also claims these accusations were 'about as often wrong as right' without a clear precision calculation.

Search channels changed mid-adjudication (the agent's tool, then Google, Brave, Yahoo and PubMed) because of quotas and bot detection. This may introduce time-dependent recall differences in NOT_FOUND decisions that are not quantified.

The paper does not cite 'Phantom References: Hallucinated Citations That Survive Peer Review' (arXiv 2607.00738). That work reports roughly one in four NeurIPS 2025 accepted papers with an unverifiable reference.

Given that omission, the discussion's claim that Agents4Science rates are 'one to two orders of magnitude above' human-authored venues, and that accepted papers here are 'an order of magnitude above' NeurIPS (based on the ~1% figure from Ansari), needs to be tempered.
Competing interest: the author operates the venue of publication. This is disclosed, but it warrants independent handling.

The human-expert correlation (rho = -0.31) is estimated on a selected top-scoring subsample (n = 78), and only 20 affected papers had human review. Inferences about human reviewers' detection are therefore weak.

The logistic-regression coefficient for the fabricated share (-25.2) comes with a note that complete separation was a concern. Given 0/58 acceptances above 10%, model stability and separation diagnostics should be reported.

decisions.rationale:
This submission audits every reference in the Agents4Science 2025 corpus. It combines a cached, reproducible bibliographic-lookup pipeline with manual adjudication of the 821 entries that pipeline could not verify. It then links the resulting labels to the organisers' automated flag, the three LLM reviewers' scores, human expert scores, acceptance decisions and self-reported AI autonomy. The panel agrees that the corpus-level linkage is the distinctive contribution. That means the evaluation of the organisers' flag against adjudicated labels (§5.3), the fabrication–score–acceptance associations (§5.5) and the reviewer-detection analysis (§5.6). Reviewer 1 places the novelty in 'adjudication across this venue's submission corpus linked to its reviews and decisions', not in the pipeline or taxonomy. Reviewer 3 reaches the same conclusion, calling the contribution 'real but incremental relative to an active literature'. Reviewer 2 judges it 'genuinely novel' and recommends acceptance. We accept that the linkage is new, but we weigh Reviewers 1 and 3 more heavily. Their concerns are specific and, in one case, backed by a cited source; Reviewer 2 acknowledges the same central weakness (single-agent adjudication) yet does not treat it as consequential.

The decisive concern, raised by all three reviewers, is that the paper's ground truth has not been independently validated. Every one of the 821 manual decisions was made by a single AI agent, the author's own. No second coder, no blinded re-adjudication and no human-checked sample is reported. The paper's central methodological argument is that automated checks cannot substitute for careful adjudication, so leaving its own adjudication unvalidated undercuts the claim it is making. The weakness matters most where judgement is involved: the EXISTS vs EXISTS_CORRUPTED boundary accounts for 43% of all fabricated references. Reviewer 1 adds a second gap. None of the 5,864 automatically verified entries was sampled for correctness, and §7 concedes that identifier-based acceptance can miss wrong authors or years. Releasing the decision log is valuable, but it does not replace reported agreement statistics.

Reviewer 3's fact-check gives this concern concrete force. Citing the arXiv version of the organisers' report, it shows that the manuscript's own reference list names 'Xian Sun' as an author of Bianchi et al. 2025, whereas the source lists 'Eric Sun'. The paper states that its own references 'were verified by resolving each identifier before submission'. That this author-list corruption survived is exactly the failure mode that §7 ('Identifier-based acceptance') acknowledges and that the paper classifies as EXISTS_CORRUPTED, which the paper counts as fabricated. It shows empirically that identifier resolution without author-level checks misses errors of the kind the paper counts. For a paper about citation integrity, this must be corrected, and every reference in the paper must be re-verified at the author, venue and year level, not just by identifier.

Several further points require revision.

- **Unmatched flagged examples (Reviewers 1 and 3).** 28 of 285 organiser-flagged examples could not be matched, 23 of them in accepted papers. They are explained only 'in the cases we could trace'. Yet the headline claim that no flagged example in an accepted paper was fabricated depends on how they are treated. Per-example evidence or explicit bounds are needed.
- **Internal inconsistency in §5.6 (Reviewer 1).** The section reports 8 affected submissions with explicit LLM statements, then describes 5 independent findings plus 'the other four'. This must be reconciled.
- **Cross-literature comparison (Reviewers 1 and 3).** §6 asserts that the gap with prior prevalence estimates is 'too large to be an artefact of method'. This is not supported, since the paper itself notes that those studies use different detection methods and outcome definitions. Either tone the claim down or support it with a sensitivity analysis on comparable definitions.
- **Related work (Reviewer 3).** Two close prior verification pipelines identified by Reviewer 3 are neither cited nor compared: RefChecker/'Phantom References' (arXiv 2607.00738), which uses a conservative identity-level definition on ML venues, and CiteAudit (arXiv 2602.23452).
- **Pre-registration timing (Reviewer 1).** The timing of the analysis plan and of the PLACEHOLDER amendment relative to data access should be documented verifiably.
- **Reviewer-model identities (Reviewer 1).** The mapping of anonymised reviewer slots to named models is inferred from matching mean scores. It should be stated as an inference.
- **Acceptance analysis (Reviewer 1).** The model adjusts only for mean LLM score, so it supports an association, not the claim that fabrication itself was penalised.
- **Corpus counts.** The organisers' report, as quoted in Reviewer 1's fact-check, gives 62 desk rejections and 253 complete, reviewed submissions. The manuscript reports 61 desk-rejected submissions and 250 with three LLM reviews. The difference may be explained by withdrawals or incomplete reviews, but it should be reconciled explicitly.

We also note, for transparency, that the author discloses operating this venue. This decision rests solely on the reviewers' grounded findings and the manuscript's content.

The work is carefully executed in many respects. The categories are well defined, Wilson intervals are used throughout, limitations are candid and all materials are released. The flag-evaluation and reviewer-detection results would be a useful contribution once the ground truth is validated. At present, however, the core labels rest on one unvalidated AI adjudicator, and the manuscript contains a demonstrable citation error of the type it measures. Both are material evidential concerns that preclude acceptance or minor revision. A major revision is required.
key_concerns: Independently validate the adjudication. Have a blinded second adjudicator (preferably human) re-code a stratified sample of the 821 manual decisions, oversampling EXISTS vs EXISTS_CORRUPTED boundary cases and NOT_FOUND decisions, and report agreement (e.g., Cohen's kappa) and the resulting uncertainty bounds on the headline prevalence figures.

Manually check a random sample of the 5,864 automatically verified entries, especially identifier-based acceptances, for author, year and venue corruption. Report the estimated miss rate and how it would revise the fabricated share.

Correct the Bianchi et al. 2025 author list ('Xian Sun' should be 'Eric Sun', per the arXiv version cited by Reviewer 3). Re-verify every reference in the manuscript at the author, venue and year level, not only by identifier resolution, and revise the §6 statement about how the paper's own references were verified.

Provide per-example evidence or explicit bounds for the 28 unmatched organiser-flagged examples, 23 of them in accepted papers. Qualify the claim that no flagged example in an accepted paper was fabricated accordingly.
Reconcile the §5.6 accounting (8 affected submissions with explicit LLM statements vs 5 independent findings plus 'the other four').
Reconcile the corpus counts with the organisers' report (62 desk rejections and 253 complete, reviewed submissions vs the manuscript's 61 and 250).

Remove or substantiate the §6 claim that the gap with prior prevalence estimates is 'too large to be an artefact of method'. Ideally, re-estimate prevalence under a definition comparable to prior audits, such as identity-level failures only.
Engage with and compare against the closest verification-pipeline prior work identified by Reviewer 3: RefChecker/'Phantom References' (arXiv 2607.00738) and CiteAudit (arXiv 2602.23452).
Document verifiably (e.g., commit hashes and timestamps) when the analysis plan and the PLACEHOLDER protocol amendment were fixed relative to data access and preliminary results.

State the mapping of anonymised reviewer slots to GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Pro and Claude Sonnet 4 explicitly as an inference from mean scores, and qualify model-specific claims (e.g., 'all five by Gemini 2.5 Pro') accordingly.

Frame the acceptance and score analyses as associational. Avoid language implying that fabrication itself was penalised, given the confounding with overall quality that the paper acknowledges, and discuss the selected sample underlying the human-score correlation.
Assess parser completeness for submissions without bracket-numbered lists, and quantify the sensitivity of headline rates to parser omissions and to the UNADJUDICABLE and PLACEHOLDER classifications.

decisions.rationale:
The revision is a substantial improvement, and the panel agrees on this. The authors added blind re-adjudication of 150 manual decisions and a blind check of 180 automatically verified entries. They also found and fixed a hanging-indent parser failure that recovered 160 references, gave per-example verdicts for the 27 unmatched organiser-flagged examples, and reconciled the §5.6 reviewer-statement accounting. The Bianchi et al. author list is corrected: Reviewer 2 confirms 'Eric Sun' against arXiv:2511.15534. The paper now engages Phantom References and CiteAudit, removes the 'too large to be an artefact of method' claim, states the reviewer-slot mapping as an inference, and frames the acceptance results as associational with separation diagnostics. On novelty, all three reviewers agree the contribution is the submission-wide adjudication linked to this venue's flag, reviews and decisions (§§5.3, 5.5, 5.6). The prior art they cite supports this: the organisers' report, GhostCite, Phantom References and CiteAudit. The verification pipeline itself is not new. We accept that framing.

We nonetheless weigh Reviewer 1's report most heavily. Its concerns are specific, checkable against the manuscript, and in several cases decisive. Reviewers 2 (minor revision) and 3 (accept) credit the new checks but do not engage with what those checks reveal.

First, the abstract was not revised and contradicts the body on nearly every headline number:
- 6,685 references vs 6,845 extracted entries
- 821 decisions vs 857
- 36.9% vs 37.8% of reviewed submissions
- 7.1% vs 7.2% of references
- 496 vs 513 fabricated references
- 8 vs 9 corrupted references in accepted papers
- 'five, all by Gemini, of 89' vs four independent findings of 91
- sensitivity 0.94 vs 0.93
- '25 flagged examples in accepted papers' vs 26 matched plus 21 unmatched

For a paper whose subject is the accuracy of bibliographic records, a summary that cannot be relied on is a serious defect.

Second, the new validation changes the substance of the findings, and the text has not caught up. §5.1 estimates that about 580 automatically accepted references carry corrupted attributes. That exceeds the 513 fabricated references found by adjudication across the whole corpus. The adjusted reference-level share for reviewed submissions is 15.9%, not 7.2%, and for accepted papers 9.9%, not 0.7%. An expected 86% of reviewed submissions carry at least one corrupted citation, against 37.8% observed. Yet the abstract and parts of §6 still describe accepted papers as 'almost clean'. They also say the organisers' 56% 'overstates' prevalence.

The paper also calls the invented-only outcome 'robust', but the blind check found 2 invented works among 180 automatically verified entries, an estimated 0.9% rate. Most of the 1,308 references in accepted papers passed through the automated stage. The claim of zero wholly invented references in accepted papers, and the invented-only paper-level prevalence, therefore need an explicit adjustment or bound. At present they rest on an assertion. Likewise, §5.3 says undetected corruption affects flagged and unflagged submissions alike, but gives no evidence on the verification-source mix in each group.

Third, several methodological claims go beyond their support.
- **Adjudicator validation.** Both adjudication and validation are agent-vs-agent. The authors disclose this candidly. All three reviewers ask for at least a small human-coded sample, and the paper's own argument that careful adjudication is the gold standard makes a human anchor important.
- **Parser upper bound.** The 101 entries with two year tokens are presented as an upper bound on residual merges. Reviewer 1 correctly notes that this does not bound them: a merged entry need not carry two years, and a genuine entry can.
- **Identity-level comparison.** This definition counts any 'wrong author list', whereas Phantom References requires a 'substantial author-list mismatch' and excludes minor name variants (Reviewer 1's fact-check of arXiv:2607.00738). It also compares all reviewed submissions here with accepted papers elsewhere.
- **Search-channel bound.** Agreement on 26 of 30 NOT_FOUND decisions does not isolate channel or timing effects, so it does not 'bound' them.
- **Pre-specification.** §6 says the categories were fixed 'before the data were seen'. §4 says the plan followed calibration on 21 papers and that PLACEHOLDER was added after 85 decisions.
- **Corpus counts.** The 253-vs-250 reconciliation is stated conditionally ('if one withdrawn submission was incomplete') rather than demonstrated.

The non-resolving DOI 10.1177/01655515241234567 is now clearly marked as an example quoted from submission 148, not a source. That concern is resolved.

The core contribution survives. However, the headline claims now need to be rebuilt around the paper's own validation results, and the abstract must be rewritten. This is more than minor editing. It requires re-estimating and reframing the central findings, so a further major revision is required. We note the disclosed competing interest: the author operates this venue. This decision rests solely on the manuscript and the reviewers' grounded findings.
key_concerns: Rewrite the abstract so every figure matches the revised body. This covers the extracted and adjudicable reference counts, the number of manual decisions, prevalence, the number of fabricated references, accepted-paper corruptions, reviewer-detection counts and denominators, flag sensitivity and precision, and the flagged examples in accepted papers. Add one auditable flow table connecting extracted, automatically accepted, manually decided, UNADJUDICABLE and analysed totals.

Reframe the headline claims around the blind check of automatically verified entries: an estimated ~580 missed corrupted references, 15.9% adjusted reference-level share for reviewed submissions, 9.9% for accepted papers, and an expected 86% paper-level. Revise or qualify 'accepted papers were almost clean' and the claim that the organisers' 56% overstates prevalence, and give uncertainty for the adjusted figures.

Estimate the effect of the 0.9% invented rate among automatically verified entries on (a) the claim of zero wholly invented references in the 48 accepted papers and (b) invented-only paper-level prevalence. Remove or qualify the statement that the invented-only outcome is robust.

Test the uniform-corruption assumption behind the adjusted estimates. Report each submission's verification-source composition, and compare flagged with unflagged submissions, to support or revise the §5.3 claim that undetected corruption does not affect the flag's precision.

Obtain a human-coded validation subset, even a modest stratified one, of both manual decisions (oversampling the NOT_FOUND vs EXISTS_CORRUPTED boundary) and automatically accepted entries, including the 19 disputed automated matches. Report agreement with the agent labels.
Replace the claim that 101 two-year-token entries are an upper bound on residual parser merges with a defensible estimate. For example, manually inspect a sample of low-ratio author-year lists.

Make the identity-level comparison with Russinovich et al. genuinely comparable: apply their 'substantial author-list mismatch' threshold and exclude minor name variants. Address the asymmetry of comparing all reviewed submissions here with accepted papers elsewhere.
Remove the claim that 26/30 NOT_FOUND agreement 'bounds' the effect of mid-adjudication search-channel changes, or support it with an analysis that isolates channel or timing.
Correct §6's statement that categories were fixed 'before the data were seen', given the calibration on 21 papers and the PLACEHOLDER amendment after 85 decisions.
Present the reconciliation of the organisers' 62/253 counts with the 61/250 OpenReview-based counts as a demonstrated classification, submission by submission, rather than a conditional one.
Make the repository, including the commit history, blind decision logs and unmatched-flag verdicts, available so the editor and readers can verify the reported statistics.

decisions.rationale:
This third-round revision resolves the substantive problems identified in round 2. We consider the remaining issues to be bounded, clearly specifiable and achievable without new data collection, apart from coding a small, already-prepared human validation sheet.

On novelty, the panel has agreed across all three rounds, and we accept its view. Reviewer 1 relies on the organisers' report (arXiv:2511.15534), and Reviewers 2 and 3 cite Phantom References (arXiv:2607.00738) and CiteAudit (arXiv:2602.23452) to show that the verification pipeline itself is not new. The genuine contribution lies elsewhere:
- a complete, evidence-logged adjudication of a single AI-first-author venue;
- an evaluation of the organisers' flag against those labels (§5.3);
- the linkage of fabrication to LLM scores, human expert scores and acceptance (§§5.5–5.6).

Reviewer 1's cited fact-check shows that Phantom References excludes minor name variants. The revised identity-level comparison now applies that threshold (15 variants excluded) and compares accepted papers with accepted papers. This resolves both the definitional mismatch and the selection asymmetry we raised in round 2.

The revision addresses the central round-2 demand, which was to rebuild the headline claims around the paper's own blind check of automatically verified entries.
- Every adjudicated rate is now labelled a lower bound.
- Table 2b gives composition-aware adjusted estimates with bootstrap intervals: 16.5% fabricated and 5.4% invented for reviewed submissions; 10.5% and 1.9% for accepted papers.
- 'Almost clean' is withdrawn, and 'no invented reference in accepted papers' becomes 'none detected, about 25 (8–57) expected undetected'.
- The claim that the organisers' 56% 'overstates' prevalence is replaced by a two-directional account of what the flag measures.
- Four earlier claims are withdrawn: the year-token 'upper bound', the search-channel 'bound', the statement that the invented-only outcome is 'robust', and the statement that categories were fixed 'before the data were seen'.
- The corpus-count reconciliation is now honestly stated as not demonstrable from public data. Because none of the four affected submissions enters any analysis, this is acceptable.

Reviewers 2 and 3 confirm that the in-body abstract matches the body figures, and Table 1b supplies the requested flow table.

We weigh Reviewer 1's major-revision report seriously, and several of its points must be fixed before acceptance. However, we judge them to be matters of qualification, completeness and verification rather than defects that undermine the contribution.

First, the stored abstract is still the round-1 text. It contradicts the body on nearly every figure and still says 'accepted papers were almost clean'. All three reviewers flag this. The authors attribute it to the revision endpoint. Whatever the cause, it must be replaced before publication, and we will verify this.

Second, there is still no human-anchored validation. Both the adjudication and its validation are agent-vs-agent. The authors disclose this candidly, and the 64-item stratified human-coding sheet is exactly the right instrument. Because the paper's central argument is that careful adjudication is the gold standard, and because the sheet is small and ready, we require that it be coded and reported as a condition of acceptance. This includes the 19 disputed automated matches, which drive the adjusted estimates. If human coding reveals systematic disagreement, the adjusted figures must be revised accordingly.

Third, the repository was private throughout review, so the decision logs, blind files and commit history could not be inspected. Appendix A is a useful mitigation. We nonetheless require editor access, or public release, before final acceptance.

Reviewer 1 also identifies overstatements that need correcting.
- **§5.3.** The claim that undetected corruption does not affect the flag comparison 'differentially' rests on similar source mixes and expected error counts. It does not establish similar within-source error rates in the flagged and unflagged groups. The sensitivity, specificity and predictive values should be stated explicitly as metrics against detected labels.
- **§7 parser extrapolation.** The extrapolation to 'at most a handful' of missing references comes from inspecting only low-ratio lists, not a sample of apparently complete ones. It should be qualified or supported with a small random sample of passing lists.
- **Appendix A.6.** It describes all 16 inspected lists as non-bracket lists, yet identifies submission 274 as a bracket list. This must be reconciled.
- **§2.** It says the blind agent re-adjudication 'plays the role of' CiteAudit's human validation. This blurs a distinction that §§5.1 and 7 correctly draw and should be reworded.

We also note an internal inconsistency. §7 reports NOT_FOUND rates by adjudication tercile of 40.5%, 32.3% and 33.3%, whereas Appendix A.5 reports 40.9%, 31.9% and 33.3%.

Finally, two further requests, raised by Reviewers 1 and 2:
- The accepted-paper adjusted estimates extrapolate rare events (1/101 Crossref, 1/5 'other') from source-level rates. Please report how many of the 180 blind-checked entries came from accepted papers, and present the accepted-paper invented estimate as a model-based projection.
- The 'expected 86%' paper-level figure should be presented less prominently, or accompanied by a submission-clustered bootstrap, since error clustering within submissions was not measured.

The disclosed competing interest (the author operates this venue) is noted. This decision rests solely on the manuscript and the reviewers' grounded findings.
key_concerns: Replace the stored (round-1) abstract with the revised abstract so that the published record carries a single abstract whose every figure matches the body: 6,849 references, 857 decisions, 37.8%/23.7%, 7.2%/3.8%, adjusted 16.5%/5.4%, 513 fabricated, 9 corruptions in 8 accepted papers, 4 of 91 independent LLM findings, sensitivity 0.93, 26 matched flagged examples in accepted papers. Remove 'accepted papers were almost clean'.

Code the released 64-item human-coding sheet with at least one independent human coder, oversampling the 19 disputed automated matches and the NOT_FOUND vs EXISTS_CORRUPTED boundary. Report agreement with both agent labels (raw and kappa). Revise the adjusted estimates in Table 2b and the text if human coding changes the per-source corruption or invention rates.

Provide the editor with access to the repository (decision logs, blind files, unmatched-flag verdicts, commit history) before final acceptance, or make it public now, so the Appendix A.3 per-source counts and headline statistics can be spot-checked.

In §5.3, state that sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV are computed against detected labels. Qualify the 'not differentially affected' claim, since similar source mixes do not establish similar within-source error rates in the flagged and unflagged groups.

Report how many of the 180 blind-checked automatically verified entries came from accepted papers. Present the accepted-paper adjusted invented estimate (about 25, 8–57) explicitly as a model-based projection from source-level rates, noting the very small event counts (1/101 Crossref, 1/5 'other').

Either de-emphasise the 'expected 86% of reviewed submissions' figure in §§5.2 and 6, or support it with a submission-clustered bootstrap, given that within-submission error clustering was not measured.

Qualify the §7 parser-omission extrapolation ('at most a handful'), which is based only on low-ratio lists, or support it by inspecting a random sample of lists that pass the current diagnostics. Reconcile Appendix A.6's description of '16 non-bracket lists' with submission 274 being a bracket list.
Reconcile the NOT_FOUND-by-tercile figures between §7 (40.5%, 32.3%, 33.3%) and Appendix A.5 (40.9%, 31.9%, 33.3%).
Reword the §2 statement that the blind agent re-adjudication 'plays the role of' CiteAudit's human validation, so that it matches the agent-vs-agent caveat given in §§5.1 and 7.

decisions.rationale:
This fourth-round revision meets one of the three conditions set in round 3 in full, meets one in form, and does not meet the third as specified. It also introduces new internal inconsistencies that must be fixed before this paper, whose subject is the accuracy of bibliographic records, can enter the published record.

Novelty has been stable across four rounds and we accept the panel's view. All three reviewers cite the organisers' report (arXiv:2511.15534), Phantom References (arXiv:2607.00738) and CiteAudit (arXiv:2602.23452) as prior art. On that basis the verification pipeline is not new. The genuine contribution is the venue-wide, evidence-logged adjudication of an AI-first-author corpus, linked to the organisers' flag, the LLM and human review scores, and the acceptance decisions (§§5.3, 5.5, 5.6). Reviewers 2 and 3 recommend acceptance and credit the revision's candour. Reviewer 1 recommends major revision on specific, checkable grounds. We weigh Reviewer 1's points most heavily because each can be verified against the manuscript, and on inspection each is correct.

The conditions from round 3 stand as follows.

(1) Stored abstract. This is resolved. The stored and body abstracts are identical.

(2) Human validation. This is not met as specified. We asked for 'at least one independent human coder'. The 64-item sheet was coded by the study's operator. The sheet also carried the agent labels, which the coder was only asked to hide (§§4, 7). The authors disclose this plainly, which we appreciate, but it is neither independent nor verifiably blind. The results also matter substantively. On the 19 disputed automated matches the operator broadly confirms the blind agent (18 of 19 defective), which supports the adjusted estimates. On the 25 disputed manual decisions, however, the human sided with the first adjudicator in only 9 (Appendix A.7: 36% category agreement; kappa -0.22 for fabricated-versus-not). The first adjudicator's labels are the ones that produce the 513 detected fabricated references. The 'approximately 94%' agreement with those labels comes from weighting two strata by a 16.7% disagreement rate. Reviewer 1 correctly notes that this rate was estimated from boundary-enriched samples, so its applicability to all 857 decisions is not established.

(3) Repository. The repository is now stated to be public. No reviewer could confirm its contents from the supplied evidence, and we will verify it before acceptance.

Reviewer 1 also identifies stale and conflicting figures, each confirmed in the text:
- §5.1 reports human-anchored source-weighted rates of 8.2% corrupted and 1.7% invented. The next sentence retains the superseded 9.7% (about 580 references) and 0.9%.
- §6 'Prevalence' still gives the adjusted reviewed-submission shares as 16.5% (13.1-20.9) and 5.4%. The abstract and Table 2b give 15.2% and 6.2%.
- §7 says 'about one in a hundred' automatically accepted entries does not exist. The final sample gives 4/180 (2.2%).
- Appendix A.6 lists submission 273 both among the low-ratio lists and in the random sample of passing lists, and does not explain the sampling frame.
- §5.3 describes 119 flagged examples as existing 'exactly as cited'. Some of these were accepted automatically, and §5.1 shows that automated acceptance can pass metadata errors. The claim should be stated relative to detected labels.

None of these problems threatens the core contribution, and none needs new data collection beyond a small, clearly bounded coding task. That is why we request minor rather than major revision. Several are nonetheless errors in headline quantitative claims, and the round-3 validation condition remains open. We therefore cannot accept in this round. We reiterate the disclosed competing interest: the author operates this venue. This decision rests solely on the manuscript and on the reviewers' grounded findings.
key_concerns: Meet the round-3 validation condition as stated. At least one human coder who is independent of the study must code the released 64-item sheet from a version that does not contain the agent labels, using only the reference strings and evidence. Report raw agreement and kappa against both agent labels, and against the operator's coding.

Because the operator's coding disagreed with the first adjudicator on most disputed manual decisions (Appendix A.7), the independent coder should also code a simple random sample of the 857 manual decisions (for example 40-50). This gives a directly estimated, non-enriched agreement with the first adjudicator's labels. Use it in place of the stratum-weighted 73%/94% figures, or to validate them.

If independent coding changes the per-source corruption or invention rates, or indicates systematic error in the first adjudicator's NOT_FOUND versus EXISTS_CORRUPTED labels, revise Table 2b and the detected counts accordingly, and give the sensitivity of the 513 detected fabricated references.

Reconcile §5.1. Remove or explicitly relabel the superseded 9.7% corrupted (about 580 references) and 0.9% invented figures now that the human-anchored source-weighted rates are 8.2% and 1.7%, and make every downstream count consistent with Table 2b.

Correct §6 'Prevalence', which still reports adjusted shares of 16.5% (13.1-20.9) and 5.4%, so that it matches the abstract and Table 2b (15.2%, 12.1-19.5, and 6.2%, 4.8-8.8). Correct §7's 'about one in a hundred' invented rate to match the final 4/180 (2.2%; source-weighted 1.7%).

Run a full consistency pass so that every number in the abstract, the body, the tables and the appendices comes from the same final analysis outputs. Report in the response letter any figure that changed.

Clarify the Appendix A.6 sampling frame. Explain why submission 273 appears both among the low-ratio lists and in the random sample of passing lists (for example, eligibility assessed after repair), and state the frame and timing precisely enough for the check to be reproduced.

In §5.3, rephrase 'exist exactly as cited' and 'no matched flagged example in an accepted paper was fabricated' as statements relative to detected labels. Note that automated acceptance can pass metadata errors and that the 21 unmatched accepted-paper examples are excluded.

Present the accepted-paper projection of about 34 (14-69) undetected invented references as a model-based projection. State explicitly that it depends on four events, two of them from a five-entry 'other' stratum, and report its value when that stratum is excluded.

Confirm that the public repository (https://github.com/publishfun-admin/agents4science-citation-audit) contains the commit history cited in §4, the decision logs, the blind files, the human-coded sheet(s) and the scripts that reproduce Table 2b. The editor will spot-check Appendix A.3 against it before acceptance. Archiving with a persistent identifier is encouraged.

decisions.rationale:
This is the fifth decision round on a paper whose contribution has been stable and agreed across all rounds. All three reviewers cite the organisers' report (arXiv:2511.15534), Phantom References (arXiv:2607.00738) and CiteAudit (arXiv:2602.23452) and agree that the verification pipeline is not new. The genuine contribution is the complete, evidence-logged adjudication of one AI-first-author venue, linked to the organisers' flag (§5.3), LLM and human review scores and acceptance decisions (§§5.5–5.6). No reviewer cites evidence that this linkage is published elsewhere. The revision also completes most of what round 4 asked for, and Reviewer 3 confirms each item against the manuscript:
- §5.1 no longer mixes superseded and human-anchored rates.
- §6 and §7 now match the abstract and Table 2b (15.2%/6.2%; 4/180 invented).
- §5.3 states precision and 'exist as cited' relative to detected labels and excludes the 21 unmatched accepted-paper examples.
- The accepted-paper projection is labelled model-based, with the sensitivity to the five-entry stratum reported (29, 9–65).
- Appendix A.6 now states its sampling frame and timing, which explains why submission 273 appears in both sets.

These points are resolved.

One condition, set in round 3 and restated in round 4, remains unmet. The authors now ask us to reconsider it. The condition was twofold. First, at least one human coder independent of the study should code a label-free version of the 64-item sheet. Second, because the operator's coding disagreed with the first adjudicator on most disputed manual decisions, a simple random sample of the 857 manual decisions should be coded to give a directly estimated, non-enriched agreement figure. The authors have drawn the random sample of 45 (seed 20261005) and released it as a reference-strings-only sheet, but they have not coded it. They argue that the author's own coding is 'independent in the sense that matters for inter-rater validation' because the author produced none of the agent labels.

Reviewer 1 recommends major revision on this ground, and its objection is unchanged from round 4. Under our persistent-dissent rule we must rule on it explicitly, and we uphold it as blocking. The authors' argument covers only half the requirement. It is true that the author did not generate the labels under test. But independence from the study's outcome is also what gives a validation its evidential force, and the author is the study's operator, the paper's sole author and the operator of the venue of publication. The blinding is also, as §§4 and 7 concede, an attestation rather than a procedure. More importantly, the concern is not procedural. Appendix A.7 shows that on the 25 disputed manual decisions the human coder agreed with the first adjudicator on only 36% of categories, with kappa −0.22 for fabricated-versus-not. Those first-adjudicator labels produce the 513 detected fabricated references and every downstream analysis. The reassuring 73%/94% figures are an extrapolation that weights boundary-enriched strata by a 16.7% disagreement rate, and nothing in the paper establishes that this rate applies to all 857 decisions (Reviewers 1 and 3 both make this point). The uncoded 45-item random sheet is exactly the instrument that would settle it. This is a validity issue documented from the manuscript itself, not an editorial point.

We weigh the reviewers as follows. Reviewer 2 (accept) acknowledges the limitation but does not engage with the Appendix A.7 disagreement. Reviewer 3 (minor revision) confirms that every other round-4 item is resolved and identifies the coding of the random sheet as the single outstanding step. Reviewer 1 (major revision) is correct on the substance. However, the remaining work is small and bounded: an external coder, 45 plus 64 label-free items, agreement statistics, and bounded revisions if agreement is low. It needs no new data collection and no redesign. That makes it a genuinely minor revision rather than grounds for rejection. We also note two further points. Reviewer 1 correctly observes that §6's statement that the venue's process 'kept out' submissions with invented references implies a causal role that §5.5 disclaims, and this should be reworded. The claim in §4 that the author's coding is independent 'in the sense that matters' overstates the case and must be qualified.

This is the final revision opportunity for this condition. It has now been stated three times, and no further major revision is available. If the next version does not report an independent, label-free human coding of the released random sample, we will have to decline the paper, because its central counts would rest on labels whose accuracy has not been independently established. The disclosed competing interest (the author operates this venue) is noted again. This decision rests solely on the manuscript and the reviewers' grounded findings.
decisions.summary_to_authors:
Thank you for a careful fifth revision. The consistency pass, the §5.3 detected-label wording, the model-based framing of the accepted-paper projection (including its sensitivity to the five-entry stratum), and the Appendix A.6 sampling-frame clarification all resolve the corresponding round-4 concerns, and all three reviewers accept the novelty of your venue-wide adjudication linked to the flag, the scores and the decisions.

We cannot accept the author's own coding as satisfying the independent-coder condition. The reason is substantive, not formal. Appendix A.7 shows weak agreement between your human reading and the first adjudicator on disputed manual decisions (36% by category; kappa −0.22 for fabricated-versus-not). The 513 detected fabricated references rest on the first adjudicator's labels, and the 73%/94% agreement figures are extrapolated from boundary-enriched strata.

You have already prepared exactly the instrument needed: a label-free simple random sample of 45 manual decisions. Please have it coded, together with a label-free version of the 64-item sheet, by a human coder who has no role in the study. Report the non-enriched agreement statistics, and revise or bound the detected counts if agreement is materially lower than your current estimate. Please also qualify the independence claim in §4 and reword the causal-sounding 'kept out' sentence in §6.

This task is small and bounded, which is why we are requesting a minor revision rather than declining the paper. Please understand, however, that this is the final opportunity to meet this condition. A resubmission without independent coding of the random sample would lead to rejection.
key_concerns: Have at least one human coder who is not the author and has no role in the study code the released reference-strings-only random sample of 45 manual decisions (independent_coder_sheet_B.csv, seed 20261005). Report raw agreement and Cohen's kappa against the first adjudicator's labels, by category and for fabricated-versus-not, with confidence intervals. Use this directly estimated figure in place of, or alongside and superseding, the stratum-weighted 73%/94% estimates in §5.1, §7 and Appendix A.7.

Have the same independent coder also code the label-free version of the 64-item sheet. Report agreement against the first adjudicator, the blind agent and the author's own coding, and state explicitly that the coder never had access to any agent labels. Record the coder's identity or role and their relationship to the study in the paper or the repository.

If independent coding of the random sample shows material disagreement with the first adjudicator (for example, fabricated-versus-not agreement well below the claimed ~94%), give a corrected estimate or explicit bounds for the 513 detected fabricated references and the headline detected rates (37.8%, 7.2%, 23.7%). State whether the §5.3 flag metrics and §§5.5–5.6 associations are robust to that error. If the per-source rates for automatically verified entries change, revise Table 2b.

Revise the sentence in §4 asserting that the author's coding is 'independent of the labels it is compared with in the sense that matters for inter-rater validation'. Present the author's coding as an operator-coded, attestation-blinded error analysis, and reserve the word 'independent' for the external coding.

In §6, reword the claim that the venue's process 'kept out the submissions with detectable invented references entirely' as an observed association (no such submission was accepted). The paper itself states that individual decisions are unobservable and that fabrication co-occurs with other weaknesses.

Ensure that the public repository contains the independent coder's completed sheets, the agreement script and outputs, and the commit history cited in §4, so that the editor can spot-check Appendix A.3, Appendix A.7 and Table 2b before final acceptance. Archiving under a persistent identifier is strongly encouraged.

concerns: Reference check: doi:10.1177/01655515241234567 is 'not_found'. In context the paper quotes it as a placeholder-pattern identifier taken from an audited submission, not as its own source, so it is consistent with the claim. It should still be explicitly marked as a non-resolving example so readers do not take it for a citation.

Reference check: arXiv:2502.01234 and arXiv:2401.12345, also quoted as placeholder-pattern identifiers from submissions, resolve to unrelated works. The registry titles are 'Homeomorphism of the Revuz correspondence for finite energy integrals' and 'Distributionally Robust Receive Combining'. This matches the paper's statement that such identifiers 'resolve to an unrelated work', but the text should say which identifier does which.

Possible citation-title drift: the paper cites Rao and Callison-Burch as 'BibTeX citation errors in scientific publishing agents'. The registry title matches this, but the fetched PDF at the EVIDENCE URL is titled 'BibTeX Citation Hallucinations in Scientific Publishing Agents: Evaluation and Mitigation', suggesting a version change the authors should reconcile.

Adjudication was performed by a single AI agent with no second coder and no inter-rater reliability estimate. The EXISTS versus EXISTS_CORRUPTED boundary involves judgement and drives about 43% of the fabricated count.

Internal count inconsistency in Q5 (Section 5.6): LLM reviews contain explicit statements in 8 affected submissions, 5 of them independent findings, yet 'in the other four' the reviewer echoes the authors' disclosure. The categories need to be reconciled.

Section 5.6 also says explicit statements occurred in 5 clean submissions, 'one by GPT-5 and three by Gemini among them', leaving one unattributed. It also claims these accusations were 'about as often wrong as right' without a clear precision calculation.

Search channels changed mid-adjudication (the agent's tool, then Google, Brave, Yahoo and PubMed) because of quotas and bot detection. This may introduce time-dependent recall differences in NOT_FOUND decisions that are not quantified.

The paper does not cite 'Phantom References: Hallucinated Citations That Survive Peer Review' (arXiv 2607.00738). That work reports roughly one in four NeurIPS 2025 accepted papers with an unverifiable reference.

Given that omission, the discussion's claim that Agents4Science rates are 'one to two orders of magnitude above' human-authored venues, and that accepted papers here are 'an order of magnitude above' NeurIPS (based on the ~1% figure from Ansari), needs to be tempered.
Competing interest: the author operates the venue of publication. This is disclosed, but it warrants independent handling.

The human-expert correlation (rho = -0.31) is estimated on a selected top-scoring subsample (n = 78), and only 20 affected papers had human review. Inferences about human reviewers' detection are therefore weak.

The logistic-regression coefficient for the fabricated share (-25.2) comes with a note that complete separation was a concern. Given 0/58 acceptances above 10%, model stability and separation diagnostics should be reported.

content.rationale: This is a structurally complete empirical paper. It states six pre-specified research questions, gives a detailed and reproducible methodology (automated resolution against several registries followed by logged manual adjudication), reports quantitative results with confidence intervals, and includes a discussion, an extensive limitations section, a related-work section and verifiable references (19 of 20 identifiers resolve, and the one that does not is a quoted example of fabrication, not a cited source). On novelty, the evidence shows the Agents4Science organisers reported only an automated flag ([1] states "approximately 44% of submissions have no hallucinated references"). Other retrieved audits target NeurIPS and USENIX papers, not this corpus. Nothing in the evidence shows that an exhaustive, manually adjudicated audit of Agents4Science references, or its link to LLM and human review outcomes, is already published. The remaining issues are ordinary quality matters for reviewers: a single AI adjudicator, small internal count discrepancies, a missing related audit, and a disclosed conflict of interest.

questions: Can the authors obtain independent, blinded adjudication of a stratified sample of unresolved entries and automated matches, and report disagreement rates and revised prevalence bounds?
How many references may be missing from unnumbered lists, and how sensitive are the headline rates to parser omissions and disputed EXISTS_CORRUPTED judgments?
What are the verdicts, or defensible bounds, for the 28 unmatched organiser-flagged examples?
Which affected submissions account for the eight-versus-five-plus-four statement in §5.6, and what establishes reviewer-model identity beyond matching mean scores?
When were the analysis plan and PLACEHOLDER amendment recorded relative to preliminary results?
strengths: §4 defines separate categories for non-existent works, corrupted citations, placeholders and unadjudicable entries, rather than equating a failed lookup with fabrication.
§5.3 reports both reference-level and paper-level evaluations of the organisers’ flag and discloses that 28 flagged examples could not be matched to parsed entries.
§7 acknowledges consequential limitations, including one AI-agent adjudicator, imperfect parser recall and automated acceptance rules that can miss metadata corruption.
weaknesses: The central labels have no reported independent validation: §4 says one AI agent adjudicated every unresolved entry, yet supplies neither blinded second-adjudicator agreement nor a manually checked sample of the 5,864 automatically verified entries. The latter is especially important because §7 concedes that identifier-based acceptance can miss wrong authors or years.

The completeness assessment in §5.1 covers bracket-numbered lists, not all 304 parsed submissions. Its minimum parsed-to-marker ratio of 0.88 also leaves potential missed entries; the effect on prevalence is unquantified.

§5.3 calls the flag’s reference-level precision 133/257, but only 257 of 285 flagged examples were matched, with 23 of the 28 unmatched in accepted papers. The broad statement that every flagged example in an accepted paper was a false alarm goes beyond the adjudicated matched examples.

§5.6 says eight affected submissions had an explicit LLM statement, then describes five independent findings and statements in 'the other four'; that accounting needs reconciliation. The assignment of anonymised reviewer slots to named models in §3 is inferred from close mean scores rather than directly established.

The acceptance model in §5.5 adjusts for mean LLM score but not the other submission qualities or decision-stage information that §7 says may accompany fabrication. It supports an association, not the claim that fabrication itself was penalised. The selected human-review sample likewise limits interpretation of its correlation.

The cross-literature magnitude claim in §6 is too confident: §6 itself says the cited audits and this study use different detection methods and outcomes. Their reported rates cannot establish that the gap is 'too large to be an artefact of method' without comparable validation.

§4 calls the plan pre-specified, but the review materials do not establish when it was fixed relative to access to corpus results. §4 also says the adjudication protocol was amended to add PLACEHOLDER; the timing and consequences of that amendment need disclosure.

The REFERENCE CHECK marks doi:10.1177/01655515241234567 as not_found. §5.7 presents it as an example of a suspect identifier in an audited submission, not as a source cited in this paper’s reference list; nevertheless, the paper should identify the exact audited entry and evidence for that example. No finding about the paper’s bibliography follows from this illustrative identifier.

The code, cache and decision-log release claimed in Data and code availability is important for reproducibility, but its contents and the paper’s primary numerical results cannot be verified from the supplied EVIDENCE.

fact_checks.claim: The organisers’ automated check reported that 56% of submissions had at least one reference it could not verify (§1).
Among 241 reviewed submissions with adjudicable references, 89 contained a fabricated reference and 361 of 5,090 references were fabricated (§5.2).
The organisers’ flag had paper-level sensitivity 0.94 and specificity 0.66 against the audit’s labels (§5.3).
One submission’s invented references appeared unchanged in a later arXiv preprint (§5.7).

content.novelty_assessment: The closest prior work is the organisers’ report, which describes the same conference and its review process (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.15534). GhostCite already studies citation validity at much larger scale (https://arxiv.org/html/2602.06718v2), while the NeurIPS audit examines fabricated citations that survived peer review (https://arxiv.org/html/2602.05930). What appears distinctive here is adjudication across this venue’s submission corpus linked to its reviews and decisions (§§3–5), not the verification pipeline or fabrication taxonomy alone. Its significance depends on the reliability of that adjudication, which the paper does not independently validate.

content.summary: This paper presents an exhaustive empirical audit of all 6,685 references across 304 submissions to Agents4Science 2025, the first conference requiring AI systems as first authors. Using a multi-stage verification pipeline followed by protocol-driven manual adjudication of 821 unverified references, the authors find that 36.9% of reviewed submissions contained at least one fabricated reference (7.1% of all references), while accepted papers contained no wholly invented references. The study also evaluates the organizers' automated web-search flag, demonstrating high sensitivity (0.94) but modest specificity (0.66) and only 51.8% reference-level precision, and shows that while fabricated citations were associated with lower LLM and human scores and rejection, reviewers rarely explicitly identified the fabrications.

strengths: Methodological completeness: Section 4 specifies a clear, pre-registered two-stage protocol combining multi-database automated matching with exhaustive manual adjudication of all 821 unverified references, with cached API responses and adjudication logs made publicly available.

Critical evaluation of existing tooling: Section 5.3 rigorously assesses the organizers' automated web-search checker, quantifying false-positive rates (nearly half of flagged examples were real works) and showing that reliance on simple web search significantly distorts prevalence estimates.

Rich empirical nuance: Section 5.5 and Section 5.6 dissect the interplay between citation fabrication, LLM reviewer scores (GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4), human expert reviews, and explicit reviewer comments, offering insightful findings into LLM reviewing blindspots.
Honest limitations: Section 7 transparently discusses the risks of negative search results, potential extraction parser loss, and single-agent adjudication.
weaknesses: Identifier lookup check: In Section 5.7, the DOI '10.1177/01655515241234567' is listed with status 'not_found' in the deterministic Crossref registry lookup. While the text cites this as an illustrative placeholder-pattern DOI from submission 173/198, the registry confirms this identifier does not resolve.

Single-agent adjudication: As acknowledged in Section 7, manual adjudication of edge cases was performed by an AI agent under human oversight rather than dual independent human annotators with inter-annotator reliability metrics (such as Cohen's kappa for annotation agreement).

Confounding in score associations: As noted in Section 6, the negative correlation between fabrication share and reviewer scores cannot cleanly separate whether reviewers penalized poor references or overall low writing quality.

Scope limited to a single non-standard venue: The findings from Agents4Science 2025 may not generalize to standard scientific workflows where human supervision and authoring dynamics differ substantially.

content.novelty_assessment: While the Agents4Science organizers previously reported an unverified 56% figure for papers with potential citation issues using an automated search check, this work provides the first exhaustive, manually adjudicated audit of the complete reference corpus. Unlike broader automated studies of the scholarly literature that rely on automated heuristics, this study inspects every unverified item, quantifies the exact false-positive profile of automated checking tools, and investigates the relationship between citation fabrication and multi-model LLM peer reviews in a live venue. The contribution is genuinely novel and provides concrete empirical benchmarks for citation integrity in agent-authored scientific writing.

content.summary: The paper presents an exhaustive audit of all references in all Agents4Science 2025 submissions (6,685 references across 304 submissions), combining an automated verification pipeline with manual adjudication of 821 unresolved references. It reports that 36.9% of reviewed submissions contain at least one fabricated reference (vs the organisers' 56% automated-flag estimate), that accepted papers are nearly clean, that the organisers' flag is a good screen but a poor measure, and that LLM reviewers almost never explicitly noticed fabrication despite giving lower scores. The work is preregistered, with released logs and cached API responses.

questions: Can a sample of the 821 adjudications (especially EXISTS_CORRUPTED vs EXISTS boundary cases) be independently re-coded by a human or second agent, with inter-rater agreement reported?
How exactly were the 28 unmatched flagged examples ruled to be checker extraction artefacts — can the per-example evidence (e.g. that a flagged title does not occur in the PDF) be published?
Is the 'Xian Sun' author error indicative of the same identifier-based acceptance weakness the paper describes in Section 7, and were this paper's own references checked at the author level?
How does your paper-level and reference-level prevalence compare to RefChecker's identity-level results on ML venues, given both audit overlapping venue types?
Can the sensitivity of the headline 36.9% to the PLACEHOLDER and UNADJUDICABLE classifications be quantified more fully (currently only a 'defective' variant is reported)?
strengths: Section 4/Methods: the verification pipeline is fully specified (ordered checks, fuzzy thresholds, quota failures and re-passes), and all API responses are cached and released, making the automated stage exactly reproducible — a standard most audits in the EVIDENCE (e.g. RefChecker [2]) do not claim.

Section 4/Analysis: the six questions and analysis plan were fixed before adjudication, deviations are flagged (the Fisher-test fallback, the PLACEHOLDER amendment), and the screening-vs-measurement distinction is handled with proper Wilson intervals throughout (Section 5).

Section 5.3/Table 3: the evaluation of the organisers' automated flag (reference-level precision 51.8%, paper-level sensitivity/specificity/kappa) is a genuinely useful methodological result, directly supporting the paper's practical recommendation in Section 6.

Section 5.6: the reviewer-detection analysis (only 5 of 89 affected papers explicitly flagged, all by one reviewer, and accusations as often wrong as right) is a novel and well-quantified finding on LLM review limitations.

Section 7: limitations are unusually honest, including the lower-bound nature of identifier-based acceptance, the selected-sample problem for human scores, and parser recall bounds via bracket-marker ratios.
weaknesses: Single adjudicator: all 821 manual decisions were made by one AI agent (the paper's own author agent), with no second coder and no reported inter-rater agreement or validation subset checked by a human — a serious gap for a paper whose central claim is that automated checks need manual adjudication (Section 4, Section 7 'One adjudicator'). Judgement calls like EXISTS vs EXISTS_CORRUPTED boundaries are unvalidated.

Citation error in the reference list: the paper cites 'Xian Sun' as an author of Bianchi et al. 2025, but the source author list [10] and the Crossref record show 'Eric Sun'. For a citation-audit paper this is an ironic and substantive error, and the registry title match in the reference check does not catch author mismatches.

The 28 unmatched flagged examples (Section 5.3) are explained as checker extraction artefacts based on the authors' own tracing of only some cases ('in the cases we could trace'); 23 of 28 are in accepted papers and directly drive the headline 'no flagged example in an accepted paper was fabricated', so this ruling is consequential and thinly evidenced.

Incomplete engagement with the closest prior verification pipelines: RefChecker/Phantom References [2] and CiteAudit [13] perform essentially the same bibliographic-resolution-plus-web-check methodology and are not cited or compared, weakening the related-work coverage (Section 2) and the novelty of the pipeline itself.

The reference check found DOI 10.1177/01655515241234567 (cited in Section 5.7) is not_found in the Crossref registry. While the paper itself presents it as an example of a placeholder-pattern fabricated identifier from the audited corpus (so its non-resolution is consistent with the paper's claim), it is nonetheless a non-resolving identifier appearing in the manuscript.

Key conference-level facts rest on a corpus the reviewer cannot independently verify: the 56% organisers' figure, the exact submission counts, the LLM reviewer means, and the submission-level examples (e.g. submission 147's arXiv propagation) have no support in the EVIDENCE beyond the organisers' report excerpts; the 56% figure in particular could not be verified from any EVIDENCE excerpt.

Section 6's claim that the gap between 7.1%/36.9% and prior literature rates is 'too large to be an artefact of method' is asserted despite the paper's own acknowledgment that prior audits rely on automated detection with different (conservative, identity-level) definitions — the comparison of prevalence across different outcome definitions and detection methods is not rigorous.

content.novelty_assessment: The general problem of hallucinated-citation auditing at scale is well covered by prior work in the EVIDENCE: Zhao et al.'s 111-million-reference audit [6], the Lancet biomedical audit [9], RefChecker/Phantom References [2], and CiteAudit's multi-agent verification benchmark [13]. The organisers' own report [10] already describes Agents4Science's reference verification agents and provides per-paper verification statistics [16]. What is genuinely new here is (a) the exhaustive, per-reference manual adjudication of a complete single AI-first-author venue, (b) the evaluation of the organisers' automated flag against ground truth, and (c) the linkage of fabrication to LLM scores, human scores and acceptance — none of which the EVIDENCE shows in prior work. The contribution is therefore real but incremental relative to an active literature the paper only partially engages (RefChecker [2] and CiteAudit [13] are uncited close relatives of its pipeline).

content.rationale:
This submission audits every reference in the Agents4Science 2025 corpus. It combines a cached, reproducible bibliographic-lookup pipeline with manual adjudication of the 821 entries that pipeline could not verify. It then links the resulting labels to the organisers' automated flag, the three LLM reviewers' scores, human expert scores, acceptance decisions and self-reported AI autonomy. The panel agrees that the corpus-level linkage is the distinctive contribution. That means the evaluation of the organisers' flag against adjudicated labels (§5.3), the fabrication–score–acceptance associations (§5.5) and the reviewer-detection analysis (§5.6). Reviewer 1 places the novelty in 'adjudication across this venue's submission corpus linked to its reviews and decisions', not in the pipeline or taxonomy. Reviewer 3 reaches the same conclusion, calling the contribution 'real but incremental relative to an active literature'. Reviewer 2 judges it 'genuinely novel' and recommends acceptance. We accept that the linkage is new, but we weigh Reviewers 1 and 3 more heavily. Their concerns are specific and, in one case, backed by a cited source; Reviewer 2 acknowledges the same central weakness (single-agent adjudication) yet does not treat it as consequential.

The decisive concern, raised by all three reviewers, is that the paper's ground truth has not been independently validated. Every one of the 821 manual decisions was made by a single AI agent, the author's own. No second coder, no blinded re-adjudication and no human-checked sample is reported. The paper's central methodological argument is that automated checks cannot substitute for careful adjudication, so leaving its own adjudication unvalidated undercuts the claim it is making. The weakness matters most where judgement is involved: the EXISTS vs EXISTS_CORRUPTED boundary accounts for 43% of all fabricated references. Reviewer 1 adds a second gap. None of the 5,864 automatically verified entries was sampled for correctness, and §7 concedes that identifier-based acceptance can miss wrong authors or years. Releasing the decision log is valuable, but it does not replace reported agreement statistics.

Reviewer 3's fact-check gives this concern concrete force. Citing the arXiv version of the organisers' report, it shows that the manuscript's own reference list names 'Xian Sun' as an author of Bianchi et al. 2025, whereas the source lists 'Eric Sun'. The paper states that its own references 'were verified by resolving each identifier before submission'. That this author-list corruption survived is exactly the failure mode that §7 ('Identifier-based acceptance') acknowledges and that the paper classifies as EXISTS_CORRUPTED, which the paper counts as fabricated. It shows empirically that identifier resolution without author-level checks misses errors of the kind the paper counts. For a paper about citation integrity, this must be corrected, and every reference in the paper must be re-verified at the author, venue and year level, not just by identifier.

Several further points require revision.

- **Unmatched flagged examples (Reviewers 1 and 3).** 28 of 285 organiser-flagged examples could not be matched, 23 of them in accepted papers. They are explained only 'in the cases we could trace'. Yet the headline claim that no flagged example in an accepted paper was fabricated depends on how they are treated. Per-example evidence or explicit bounds are needed.
- **Internal inconsistency in §5.6 (Reviewer 1).** The section reports 8 affected submissions with explicit LLM statements, then describes 5 independent findings plus 'the other four'. This must be reconciled.
- **Cross-literature comparison (Reviewers 1 and 3).** §6 asserts that the gap with prior prevalence estimates is 'too large to be an artefact of method'. This is not supported, since the paper itself notes that those studies use different detection methods and outcome definitions. Either tone the claim down or support it with a sensitivity analysis on comparable definitions.
- **Related work (Reviewer 3).** Two close prior verification pipelines identified by Reviewer 3 are neither cited nor compared: RefChecker/'Phantom References' (arXiv 2607.00738), which uses a conservative identity-level definition on ML venues, and CiteAudit (arXiv 2602.23452).
- **Pre-registration timing (Reviewer 1).** The timing of the analysis plan and of the PLACEHOLDER amendment relative to data access should be documented verifiably.
- **Reviewer-model identities (Reviewer 1).** The mapping of anonymised reviewer slots to named models is inferred from matching mean scores. It should be stated as an inference.
- **Acceptance analysis (Reviewer 1).** The model adjusts only for mean LLM score, so it supports an association, not the claim that fabrication itself was penalised.
- **Corpus counts.** The organisers' report, as quoted in Reviewer 1's fact-check, gives 62 desk rejections and 253 complete, reviewed submissions. The manuscript reports 61 desk-rejected submissions and 250 with three LLM reviews. The difference may be explained by withdrawals or incomplete reviews, but it should be reconciled explicitly.

We also note, for transparency, that the author discloses operating this venue. This decision rests solely on the reviewers' grounded findings and the manuscript's content.

The work is carefully executed in many respects. The categories are well defined, Wilson intervals are used throughout, limitations are candid and all materials are released. The flag-evaluation and reviewer-detection results would be a useful contribution once the ground truth is validated. At present, however, the core labels rest on one unvalidated AI adjudicator, and the manuscript contains a demonstrable citation error of the type it measures. Both are material evidential concerns that preclude acceptance or minor revision. A major revision is required.
key_concerns_to_address: Independently validate the adjudication. Have a blinded second adjudicator (preferably human) re-code a stratified sample of the 821 manual decisions, oversampling EXISTS vs EXISTS_CORRUPTED boundary cases and NOT_FOUND decisions, and report agreement (e.g., Cohen's kappa) and the resulting uncertainty bounds on the headline prevalence figures.

Manually check a random sample of the 5,864 automatically verified entries, especially identifier-based acceptances, for author, year and venue corruption. Report the estimated miss rate and how it would revise the fabricated share.

Correct the Bianchi et al. 2025 author list ('Xian Sun' should be 'Eric Sun', per the arXiv version cited by Reviewer 3). Re-verify every reference in the manuscript at the author, venue and year level, not only by identifier resolution, and revise the §6 statement about how the paper's own references were verified.

Provide per-example evidence or explicit bounds for the 28 unmatched organiser-flagged examples, 23 of them in accepted papers. Qualify the claim that no flagged example in an accepted paper was fabricated accordingly.
Reconcile the §5.6 accounting (8 affected submissions with explicit LLM statements vs 5 independent findings plus 'the other four').
Reconcile the corpus counts with the organisers' report (62 desk rejections and 253 complete, reviewed submissions vs the manuscript's 61 and 250).

Remove or substantiate the §6 claim that the gap with prior prevalence estimates is 'too large to be an artefact of method'. Ideally, re-estimate prevalence under a definition comparable to prior audits, such as identity-level failures only.
Engage with and compare against the closest verification-pipeline prior work identified by Reviewer 3: RefChecker/'Phantom References' (arXiv 2607.00738) and CiteAudit (arXiv 2602.23452).
Document verifiably (e.g., commit hashes and timestamps) when the analysis plan and the PLACEHOLDER protocol amendment were fixed relative to data access and preliminary results.

State the mapping of anonymised reviewer slots to GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Pro and Claude Sonnet 4 explicitly as an inference from mean scores, and qualify model-specific claims (e.g., 'all five by Gemini 2.5 Pro') accordingly.

Frame the acceptance and score analyses as associational. Avoid language implying that fabrication itself was penalised, given the confounding with overall quality that the paper acknowledges, and discuss the selected sample underlying the human-score correlation.
Assess parser completeness for submissions without bracket-numbered lists, and quantify the sensitivity of headline rates to parser omissions and to the UNADJUDICABLE and PLACEHOLDER classifications.

content.summary: The revision audits references in Agents4Science 2025 submissions, compares its labels with the organisers’ automated flag, and relates citation failures to review scores and decisions. It adds blind agent re-adjudication, a check of automatically verified entries, improved parsing, and corrected analyses. Those checks also reveal enough missed citation errors that several headline interpretations need substantial revision.

What do independent human checks find in stratified samples of both manual decisions and automatically accepted entries, particularly the 19 disputed automated matches?
How do the two invented works found among automatically accepted entries change invented-only prevalence and the probability that accepted papers contain an invented reference?
What are the organiser flag’s precision, specificity, and paper-level comparison after accounting for estimated missed errors separately in flagged and unflagged submissions?
Which author-list discrepancies meet Phantom References’ substantial-mismatch criterion, and how does the comparison change when both studies use comparable selection of papers?
Can the withdrawal classifications, commit history, parser-omission assessment, and released validation files be made independently inspectable?
strengths: §§4–5.1 directly address the previous round’s principal concern by reporting stratified blind re-adjudication, agreement for both categories and the binary outcome, and checks of automatically accepted entries; §7 correctly says this measures agreement between agents, not human accuracy.
§§4–5.1 identify and repair a consequential hanging-indent parsing failure, report the 160 additional references it yielded, and extend recall diagnostics beyond bracket-numbered lists.
§5.3 now bounds precision over unmatched flagged examples, distinguishes matched from unmatched examples in accepted papers, and reports a per-example classification.
§§5.5–5.6 reconcile the reviewer-statement counts, identify the reviewer-slot mapping as an inference, and frame the acceptance model as associational rather than causal.
weaknesses: The abstract remains largely unrevised and materially contradicts the body: it reports 6,685 references, 821 decisions, 36.9% of reviewed papers affected, 7.1% of references fabricated, 8 corrupted accepted-paper references, 5 independent reviewer findings, and 496 fabricated references. §§5.1–5.7 instead report 6,845 extracted entries, 857 decisions, 37.8%, 7.2%, 9 accepted-paper corruptions, 4 independent findings, and 513 fabricated references. A reader cannot rely on the paper’s summary.

The new validation exposes a major measurement failure rather than merely narrowing uncertainty. §5.1 estimates that about 580 automatically accepted references have corrupted attributes, versus 513 fabricated references found by adjudication across the whole corpus. The adjusted reviewed-submission rate in §5.2 is 15.9%, not the abstract’s 7.1% or the prominently discussed 7.2%. Claims in §§5.3 and 6 that the organiser flag overstates actual fabrication, and that accepted papers are nearly clean, need to be reformulated around this result and its uncertainty.

§§5.1–5.2 call the invented-only outcome robust, but the blind check found two invented works among 180 automatically verified entries and estimates a 0.9% invented rate in that stratum. The consequences for the claim of zero invented references in accepted papers, and for invented-only paper-level prevalence, are not estimated. Likewise, §5.3 asserts that undetected corruption affects flagged and unflagged papers alike without showing the relevant verification-source distributions.

§4 and §7 still provide no human validation of either set of agent decisions. The 180-entry automated-match check is small for source-specific and outcome-specific conclusions, and agreement between two agent instances cannot establish accuracy against a human-checked standard. The adjusted paper-level estimate of 86% in §5.2 also assumes errors are distributed across submissions without directly measuring their clustering.

The parser sensitivity analysis in §§5.1 and 7 treats 101 entries containing two year tokens as an upper bound on residual merges. A merged entry need not contain two distinct year tokens, while one genuine entry can contain two; the reported year-token proxy therefore does not establish an upper bound on omissions.

The purportedly comparable identity-level analysis in §§5.2 and 6 counts a 'wrong author list', whereas the cited Phantom References definition requires a 'substantial author-list mismatch' and excludes minor name variants (https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.00738). The paper does not show that its 279 failures meet that threshold. Its further comparison of all reviewed submissions here with accepted papers elsewhere is selection-asymmetric.

§3’s reconciliation of 253 complete submissions in the organisers’ report with 250 reviewed submissions in the analysed data is explicitly conditional—'if one withdrawn submission was incomplete'—rather than a demonstrated classification. §4 supplies commit identifiers for pre-specification, but neither their timing nor the claimed release contents can be verified from the supplied EVIDENCE; the plan also followed calibration on 21 papers, and PLACEHOLDER was added after 85 decisions. §6 should not say the categories were fixed before the data were seen.

REFERENCE CHECK marks doi:10.1177/01655515241234567 as 'not_found'. §5.7 explicitly identifies it as a non-resolving example quoted from an audited submission, not a source in this paper’s bibliography, so this is not evidence of a fabricated bibliography entry here. It remains a serious non-resolving identifier in a substantive example: the submission-entry attribution and its interpretation depend on the released underlying record, which is not available in the supplied EVIDENCE.

§7 says agreement on 26 of 30 sampled NOT_FOUND decisions 'bounds the effect' of changing search channels. Agreement from a sample that does not isolate channel or timing effects does not supply such a bound.
