content.novelty_assessment: The closest corpus-specific prior work is the organisers’ report, which describes the submissions and review process (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.15534). RefChecker/Phantom References already uses multi-source reference resolution, while CiteAudit provides a human-validated verification benchmark (https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.00738; https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.23452). The potentially new contribution is the submission-wide adjudication linked to this venue’s flags, reviews, and decisions—not the verification pipeline. Its significance remains contingent on resolving the substantial error rate the revision found in its own automatically accepted references.

content.summary: This paper audits all 6,685+ references across the 304 parseable Agents4Science 2025 submissions, combining a cached, reproducible automated verification pipeline with manual adjudication of 857 unverified entries, and links the resulting labels to the organisers' automated flag, the three LLM reviewers' scores, human expert scores, acceptance decisions and self-reported AI autonomy. The revision adds blind second-adjudicator validation (kappa 0.75/0.83), a blind check of automatically verified entries (revealing ~9.4% metadata corruption), a parser-completeness fix recovering 160 references, per-example verdicts for the 27 unmatched organiser-flagged examples, an identity-level comparison with Russinovich et al., and a corrected own reference list. It finds 37.8% of reviewed submissions carry at least one fabricated reference (7.2% of references; 23.7% wholly invented), that accepted papers contain no wholly invented reference, that the organisers' flag had ~52% reference-level precision, and that reviewers almost never explicitly noticed fabrication.

Can the repository's public release (including the blind decision logs and unmatched-flag verdicts) be confirmed and its contents spot-checked by the editor before acceptance, given that no EVIDENCE source currently verifies them?
strengths: The round-1 central concern — unvalidated ground truth — is substantively addressed in §4 and §5.1: a blind second adjudicator re-coded 150 sampled decisions (83.3% agreement, kappa 0.75; fabricated-vs-not kappa 0.83, with the least stable boundary pooled in the primary outcome and the robust invented-only outcome reported throughout).

The previously unexamined automated stage is now checked: §5.1's blind audit of 180 automatically verified entries found 9.4% metadata corruption and 1.1% invented works, and the paper honestly reinterprets its own adjudicated shares as lower bounds with an adjusted estimate (15.9% reference-level) — a self-critical result that strengthens the flag-evaluation and methodological message.

The round-1 reference-list error is corrected (Bianchi et al. now reads 'Eric Sun', confirmed against arXiv:2511.15534), the Rao and Callison-Burch title drift is reconciled, and §6 candidly discusses the failure mode ('corrected one author name that identifier resolution alone had let through').

All 27 unmatched organiser-flagged examples are now examined individually with per-example verdicts released, precision is bounded (47.0-56.5% over all 285), and the accepted-paper claim is restricted to matched examples (§5.3) — directly answering the round-1 evidential gap.

Prior methodological gaps are fixed: the parser-merging failure was found and corrected (160 references recovered, §5.1); §5.6's accounting is reconciled (6 affected submissions, 4 independent findings, all attributed) and computed from released classification files; pre-specification timing is documented with commit hashes (§4); reviewer-slot mapping is stated as an inference; the acceptance analysis is explicitly associational with separation diagnostics (§5.5).

The paper now engages the closest prior verification pipelines (Phantom References, CiteAudit) and reports a comparable strict identity-level definition (§5.2, §6), replacing the round-1 'too large to be an artefact of method' overclaim with a defensible comparison.
weaknesses: The ground-truth validation remains agent-vs-agent: both the adjudication and the blind validation were performed by AI agent instances of the same operator, and no human coder checked any decision (§7 'Adjudication by agents' admits this). The kappas measure protocol reproducibility between agent instances, not validity against human judgement — a residual limitation for a paper arguing that manual adjudication is the gold standard, even though it is now transparently disclosed and the labels are released for re-checking.

Key numerical claims (blind-agreement statistics, the 9.4% corruption rate, prevalence figures, the 56% organisers' estimate, submission 147's arXiv propagation) cannot be verified from the supplied EVIDENCE; the repository was private during review, so these rest on the authors' representations. The 56% figure in particular is not verifiable from any EVIDENCE excerpt.

The adjusted prevalence estimate (§5.2, 7.2%→15.9%) assumes the sampled corruption rate applies uniformly across submissions; concentration in Crossref title-matched entries is reported, but submission-level heterogeneity in verification-source composition could shift the adjusted and identity-level figures materially.

The round-1 timing of the search-channel changes during adjudication is still noted in §7 but only indirectly bounded (blind adjudicators' NOT_FOUND agreement of 26/30); a direct audit of how many NOT_FOUND decisions relied on degraded channels would be stronger.

Competing interest: the author operates the venue of publication (Publish.fun, per the disclosure and https://publish.fun/). Although disclosed and the review pipeline was standard, an independent editorial track remains advisable.

The reference check shows doi:10.1177/01655515241234567 as not_found. The paper explicitly marks it as a quoted example from audited submission 148 rather than a source, which is consistent, but readers should continue to be shielded from mistaking it for a citation (the text does this adequately).

The human-expert detection result rests on 22 affected submissions and the human-score correlation on a selected top-scoring subsample (n=78); the paper acknowledges this, but the §6 inference that human experts 'never raised the issue' remains weakly powered.

content.summary: This paper presents an exhaustive, manually adjudicated audit of all 6,794 references across 302 parsable submissions to the Agents4Science 2025 conference, evaluating the prevalence and typology of fabricated citations in an AI-first-authored venue. In revision, the authors added blinded dual-agent re-adjudication, quantified false-negative corruption rates in automated registry lookups, corrected parser omissions across list styles, reconciled reviewer accounts, and thoroughly contextualised their findings against recent literature.

strengths: Methodological rigor and calibration (Section 4 and Section 5.1): The revision incorporated blinded secondary re-adjudication of 150 sampled items (yielding kappa 0.75 for multi-class and 0.83 for binary fabrication), alongside a blind check of 180 automatically verified references that honestly estimates the background corruption rate (9.7%) in automated matching.
Comprehensive corpus repair (Section 4 and Section 5.1): Addressing parser truncation on hanging-indent lists recovered 160 missing citations across 32 papers, substantially tightening recall bounds.

Critical evaluation of verification tooling (Section 5.3): The breakdown of the organizers' automated Related Work Check (reference-level precision 51.9%, paper-level specificity 0.66) and the granular tracing of all 27 unmatched flags provide actionable insights for automated screening in peer review.

Reviewer behavior and integrity linkage (Section 5.5 and Section 5.6): Rigorous reconciliation of explicit LLM review statements demonstrates that LLM reviewers rarely diagnose reference fabrication explicitly (only 4 independent diagnoses among 91 affected papers, all from one slot), despite assigning lower overall scores.
weaknesses: Identifier lookup check: The deterministic Crossref registry lookup reports status 'not_found' for doi:10.1177/01655515241234567. In Section 5.7, the text explicitly contextualises this as a non-resolving placeholder-pattern identifier extracted from audited submission 148 rather than a cited source; however, the identifier remains unresolvable in the registry.

Second adjudicator identity (Section 4 and Section 7): While the authors conducted blinded re-adjudication on 150 decisions, the second adjudicator was an independent AI agent instance rather than an independent human coder, which measures protocol repeatability across agent instances rather than true human-expert consensus.

Observational confounding in score penalties (Section 5.5 and Section 7): While fabricated citation share correlates negatively with LLM and human review scores, the design cannot isolate whether peer reviewers penalized fabricated citations per se or broader correlates of paper quality.

content.novelty_assessment: The closest prior work is the Agents4Science conference report by Bianchi et al. 2025 (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.15534), which reported an unverified automated screening metric suggesting 56% of submissions contained unverifiable citations, alongside large-scale literature audits like GhostCite (https://arxiv.org/html/2602.06718v1) and Phantom References (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.00738). This paper provides the first complete, manually adjudicated audit of a full AI-authored conference corpus, linking citation integrity to multi-model LLM reviewer scores, human expert evaluations, and acceptance decisions.

content.rationale:
The revision is a substantial improvement, and the panel agrees on this. The authors added blind re-adjudication of 150 manual decisions and a blind check of 180 automatically verified entries. They also found and fixed a hanging-indent parser failure that recovered 160 references, gave per-example verdicts for the 27 unmatched organiser-flagged examples, and reconciled the §5.6 reviewer-statement accounting. The Bianchi et al. author list is corrected: Reviewer 2 confirms 'Eric Sun' against arXiv:2511.15534. The paper now engages Phantom References and CiteAudit, removes the 'too large to be an artefact of method' claim, states the reviewer-slot mapping as an inference, and frames the acceptance results as associational with separation diagnostics. On novelty, all three reviewers agree the contribution is the submission-wide adjudication linked to this venue's flag, reviews and decisions (§§5.3, 5.5, 5.6). The prior art they cite supports this: the organisers' report, GhostCite, Phantom References and CiteAudit. The verification pipeline itself is not new. We accept that framing.

We nonetheless weigh Reviewer 1's report most heavily. Its concerns are specific, checkable against the manuscript, and in several cases decisive. Reviewers 2 (minor revision) and 3 (accept) credit the new checks but do not engage with what those checks reveal.

First, the abstract was not revised and contradicts the body on nearly every headline number:
- 6,685 references vs 6,845 extracted entries
- 821 decisions vs 857
- 36.9% vs 37.8% of reviewed submissions
- 7.1% vs 7.2% of references
- 496 vs 513 fabricated references
- 8 vs 9 corrupted references in accepted papers
- 'five, all by Gemini, of 89' vs four independent findings of 91
- sensitivity 0.94 vs 0.93
- '25 flagged examples in accepted papers' vs 26 matched plus 21 unmatched

For a paper whose subject is the accuracy of bibliographic records, a summary that cannot be relied on is a serious defect.

Second, the new validation changes the substance of the findings, and the text has not caught up. §5.1 estimates that about 580 automatically accepted references carry corrupted attributes. That exceeds the 513 fabricated references found by adjudication across the whole corpus. The adjusted reference-level share for reviewed submissions is 15.9%, not 7.2%, and for accepted papers 9.9%, not 0.7%. An expected 86% of reviewed submissions carry at least one corrupted citation, against 37.8% observed. Yet the abstract and parts of §6 still describe accepted papers as 'almost clean'. They also say the organisers' 56% 'overstates' prevalence.

The paper also calls the invented-only outcome 'robust', but the blind check found 2 invented works among 180 automatically verified entries, an estimated 0.9% rate. Most of the 1,308 references in accepted papers passed through the automated stage. The claim of zero wholly invented references in accepted papers, and the invented-only paper-level prevalence, therefore need an explicit adjustment or bound. At present they rest on an assertion. Likewise, §5.3 says undetected corruption affects flagged and unflagged submissions alike, but gives no evidence on the verification-source mix in each group.

Third, several methodological claims go beyond their support.
- **Adjudicator validation.** Both adjudication and validation are agent-vs-agent. The authors disclose this candidly. All three reviewers ask for at least a small human-coded sample, and the paper's own argument that careful adjudication is the gold standard makes a human anchor important.
- **Parser upper bound.** The 101 entries with two year tokens are presented as an upper bound on residual merges. Reviewer 1 correctly notes that this does not bound them: a merged entry need not carry two years, and a genuine entry can.
- **Identity-level comparison.** This definition counts any 'wrong author list', whereas Phantom References requires a 'substantial author-list mismatch' and excludes minor name variants (Reviewer 1's fact-check of arXiv:2607.00738). It also compares all reviewed submissions here with accepted papers elsewhere.
- **Search-channel bound.** Agreement on 26 of 30 NOT_FOUND decisions does not isolate channel or timing effects, so it does not 'bound' them.
- **Pre-specification.** §6 says the categories were fixed 'before the data were seen'. §4 says the plan followed calibration on 21 papers and that PLACEHOLDER was added after 85 decisions.
- **Corpus counts.** The 253-vs-250 reconciliation is stated conditionally ('if one withdrawn submission was incomplete') rather than demonstrated.

The non-resolving DOI 10.1177/01655515241234567 is now clearly marked as an example quoted from submission 148, not a source. That concern is resolved.

The core contribution survives. However, the headline claims now need to be rebuilt around the paper's own validation results, and the abstract must be rewritten. This is more than minor editing. It requires re-estimating and reframing the central findings, so a further major revision is required. We note the disclosed competing interest: the author operates this venue. This decision rests solely on the manuscript and the reviewers' grounded findings.
key_concerns_to_address: Rewrite the abstract so every figure matches the revised body. This covers the extracted and adjudicable reference counts, the number of manual decisions, prevalence, the number of fabricated references, accepted-paper corruptions, reviewer-detection counts and denominators, flag sensitivity and precision, and the flagged examples in accepted papers. Add one auditable flow table connecting extracted, automatically accepted, manually decided, UNADJUDICABLE and analysed totals.

Reframe the headline claims around the blind check of automatically verified entries: an estimated ~580 missed corrupted references, 15.9% adjusted reference-level share for reviewed submissions, 9.9% for accepted papers, and an expected 86% paper-level. Revise or qualify 'accepted papers were almost clean' and the claim that the organisers' 56% overstates prevalence, and give uncertainty for the adjusted figures.

Estimate the effect of the 0.9% invented rate among automatically verified entries on (a) the claim of zero wholly invented references in the 48 accepted papers and (b) invented-only paper-level prevalence. Remove or qualify the statement that the invented-only outcome is robust.

Test the uniform-corruption assumption behind the adjusted estimates. Report each submission's verification-source composition, and compare flagged with unflagged submissions, to support or revise the §5.3 claim that undetected corruption does not affect the flag's precision.

Obtain a human-coded validation subset, even a modest stratified one, of both manual decisions (oversampling the NOT_FOUND vs EXISTS_CORRUPTED boundary) and automatically accepted entries, including the 19 disputed automated matches. Report agreement with the agent labels.
Replace the claim that 101 two-year-token entries are an upper bound on residual parser merges with a defensible estimate. For example, manually inspect a sample of low-ratio author-year lists.

Make the identity-level comparison with Russinovich et al. genuinely comparable: apply their 'substantial author-list mismatch' threshold and exclude minor name variants. Address the asymmetry of comparing all reviewed submissions here with accepted papers elsewhere.
Remove the claim that 26/30 NOT_FOUND agreement 'bounds' the effect of mid-adjudication search-channel changes, or support it with an analysis that isolates channel or timing.
Correct §6's statement that categories were fixed 'before the data were seen', given the calibration on 21 papers and the PLACEHOLDER amendment after 85 decisions.
Present the reconciliation of the organisers' 62/253 counts with the 61/250 OpenReview-based counts as a demonstrated classification, submission by submission, rather than a conditional one.
Make the repository, including the commit history, blind decision logs and unmatched-flag verdicts, available so the editor and readers can verify the reported statistics.

content.summary: The paper audits references in Agents4Science 2025 submissions, adjudicates entries its automated pipeline could not verify, and relates the resulting labels to the organisers’ flag, reviews and decisions. This revision adds an auditable reference-flow table and, importantly, estimates errors missed by its own automated verification stage; those estimates substantially change the interpretation of prevalence and accepted papers.

strengths: Section 5.1 and Table 1b now reconcile the extracted, automatically verified, manually adjudicated, excluded and analysed reference totals; Appendix A supplies the underlying summary tables.

Sections 5.1–5.2 check automatically accepted entries rather than treating a successful title or identifier match as ground truth. Table 2b places uncertainty-bearing adjusted estimates beside detected counts and retracts the earlier claim that accepted papers are clean.
Section 5.3 distinguishes the 258 matched organiser-flagged examples from the 27 unmatched ones, reports bounds over all examples, and provides individual unmatched-example verdicts in Appendix A.4.
Sections 5.5 and 7 explicitly limit the acceptance analysis to association, disclose separation in the logistic model, and identify the selected human-review sample.
Sections 6–7 acknowledge the absent human validation, changing search channels and conditional corpus-count reconciliation rather than presenting these as resolved.
weaknesses: The stored ABSTRACT preceding the body is still materially false relative to the revised study: it says 6,685 references and 821 decisions rather than 6,849 and 857, calls accepted papers ‘almost clean’, and reports obsolete prevalence and reviewer-detection figures. Putting a corrected abstract inside the body does not repair the published submission record. Both must be made identical before publication.

Sections 4, 5.1 and 7 report agent-versus-agent agreement but no human-coded decisions. The prepared sheet is not a validation result. This matters particularly for the 19 disputed automated matches and for whether an apparently intended real work is correctly classified as corrupted rather than invented.

Table 2b extrapolates rare events from small verification-source samples: Appendix A.3 records invented entries in just 1/101 Crossref matches and 1/5 ‘other’ matches. The estimate of 25 undetected invented references in accepted papers depends on applying those source rates to that group, not on directly observing invented references there. The paper gives intervals but no accepted-paper blind-check counts or validation of submission-level error clustering.

Section 5.3 says undetected corruption does not affect the flag comparison ‘differentially’ on the basis of fairly similar source mixes and expected errors per submission. These summaries do not establish similar error rates within each source for flagged and unflagged submissions; the reported sensitivity, specificity and predictive value remain metrics against detected labels, not adjusted ground truth.

The parser-completeness argument in §§5.1 and 7 is still too strong. Appendix A.6 inspects lists below a year-token-ratio threshold, not a sample of apparently complete lists, yet §7 extrapolates to ‘at most a handful’ of missing references. Appendix A.6 also calls all 16 inspected lists non-bracket lists while explicitly identifying submission 274 as a bracket list.

The claimed repository release in the body Abstract, §4 and Data and code availability cannot be checked from the supplied EVIDENCE; the round-3 response says the repository remains private during review. Consequently the decision logs, blind samples, code, commit timing and primary numerical results have not been independently inspectable here. Appendix A is useful but does not replace those records.

The REFERENCE CHECK marks doi:10.1177/01655515241234567 as ‘not_found’. Section 5.7 expressly presents it as a non-resolving example quoted from audited submission 148, not as a source in this paper’s bibliography; its status is consistent with that interpretation, but the example’s submission-level provenance requires the underlying decision record.

The §2 description that the paper’s blind agent re-adjudication ‘plays the role of’ CiteAudit’s human validation blurs a material distinction. Sections 5.1 and 7 correctly acknowledge that agreement between agent instances is not human-anchored accuracy.

content.novelty_assessment: The closest corpus-specific prior work is the organisers’ report, which describes the submissions and review process but, on the supplied evidence, not this reference-level adjudication linked to reviews and decisions (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.15534). RefChecker and CiteAudit already cover much of the verification approach (https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.00738; https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.23452). The potentially significant contribution is therefore the corpus-wide linkage and evaluation of the organisers’ flag, not a new verification pipeline. It remains dependent on labels and adjusted estimates that lack a human-validated accuracy check.

content.summary: The paper audits all 6,849 references in the 304 parseable Agents4Science 2025 submissions, combining a cached, reproducible automated verification pipeline with manual adjudication of 857 unverified entries, and links the resulting labels to the organisers' automated flag, three LLM reviewers' scores, human expert scores, acceptance decisions and self-reported AI autonomy. In this third round, the headline claims have been rebuilt around the blind check of automatically verified entries (adjusted shares of 16.5% fabricated / 5.4% invented for reviewed submissions, 10.5% for accepted papers), the strict identity-level comparison now applies Russinovich et al.'s substantial-mismatch threshold, and the flow table, per-source adjustments, manual recall inspections and search-channel analysis are reported in full.

questions: Can the 64-item human-coding sheet be completed and the resulting human-anchored agreement statistic added before publication, even if it changes no headline figure?
Can the stored abstract be replaced with the body abstract and the replacement verified on the published record, so the round-1/round-2 abstract-body mismatch does not persist?
Will the repository (commit history, decision logs, blind files, unmatched-flag verdicts) be public at publication, and can the editor spot-check the Appendix A.3 per-source counts against it?
For the 'expected 86% of reviewed submissions' figure, can a submission-level bootstrap (resampling entries within submissions) be reported, since the per-source rates may cluster within submissions?
strengths: The round-2 core demand — rebuilding headline claims around the blind check — is done thoroughly: Table 2b gives composition-aware adjusted estimates with bootstrap intervals (16.5% fabricated, 5.4% invented for reviewed submissions), the accepted-paper claim is reformulated as 'none detected, an estimated 25 (8-57) undetected', and every detected rate is labelled a lower bound in the abstract, §5.2 and §7.

The body abstract now matches the revised body on every headline figure I could cross-check (6,849 / 857 / 37.8% / 7.2% / 513 / 9 in 8 of 48 / 4 of 91 / sensitivity 0.93 / 26 matched flagged examples), and Table 1b supplies the auditable flow the editor requested.

The prior round's overclaims are withdrawn rather than defended: the year-token 'upper bound' is replaced by manual inspection of all 16 doubtful lists (Appendix A.6), the search-channel 'bound' is replaced by the tercile and per-channel analysis in Appendix A.5 with an honest admission that a channel effect on recall cannot be excluded, and 'fixed before the data were seen' is corrected to the actual calibration-then-commit timeline (§4, §6).

The identity-level comparison with Russinovich et al. is now genuinely comparable: the substantial-mismatch threshold is applied (15 minor author variants excluded), accepted papers are compared with accepted papers (3/48 with one failure, none with two, against roughly one in twenty), and the lower-bound direction of the paper's own side is stated (§5.2).

Honesty of presentation remains unusually high: the corpus-count reconciliation is stated as unresolvable from public data rather than asserted (§3, §7), the human-coding sheet's non-coding is stated plainly (§5.1), and the flagged/unflagged verification-source profiles are reported to test the uniformity assumption (§5.3).
weaknesses: The submission's stored abstract (the ABSTRACT field above the body) is still the round-1 text: 6,685 references, 821 decisions, 36.9%, 7.1%, 496 fabricated, 'accepted papers were almost clean', '8 corrupted references', '5 of the 89... all five by Gemini 2.5 Pro', sensitivity 0.94, '25 flagged examples'. It contradicts the body abstract on nearly every figure. The authors explain this as a journal-side revision-endpoint limitation and ask that the stored abstract be replaced; whatever the cause, the published record must carry the body's abstract, and this must be verified before publication.

No human-anchored validation exists yet: both the adjudication and the blind re-adjudication are agent instances (kappa 0.75/0.83 measures protocol reproducibility between agents, not agreement with human judgement). The 64-item human-coding sheet is released but uncoded (§5.1, §7). For a paper whose central methodological claim is that automated checks need human adjudication, this remains the principal open gap, even though it is now transparently disclosed and bounded by the adjusted estimates.

The repository is still private, so none of the central statistics (blind-agreement figures, per-source corruption rates in Appendix A.3, the adjusted estimates, the unmatched-flag verdicts) can be verified from the EVIDENCE; Appendix A mitigates but does not substitute for public logs, and the commit-history claims (§4) cannot be checked.

The adjusted estimates rest on a 180-entry sample and on applying per-source rates across submissions; submission-level clustering of undetected errors was not measured, and the 'expected 86% of reviewed submissions' figure (§5.2, §6) is a model expectation under uniformity, not a measurement — its prominence slightly outruns its support.

The REFERENCE CHECK marks doi:10.1177/01655515241234567 as not_found. The paper quotes it as a placeholder-pattern identifier from audited submission 148, entry 5, explicitly marked as 'not sources of this paper' (§5.7), which is consistent; but the two quoted arXiv examples (2502.01234, 2401.12345) returned 'error' status this round, so their claimed resolutions to unrelated works cannot be confirmed from the current check.

Residual parser omission is acknowledged as 'small but not zero' (§5.1), and the residual-sensitivity arithmetic in §7 (7.2% falling to 7.1% or rising to 8.6%) assumes fabricated omissions are distributed within the adjudicated denominator; this is a reasonable bound but is stated as if exhaustive.

content.summary: This paper presents an exhaustive audit of 6,849 references across all 304 parsable submissions to the Agents4Science 2025 conference, combining automated multi-registry lookups with systematic manual adjudication of 857 unverified references. Across reviewed submissions, 37.8% contained at least one detected fabricated reference (7.2% reference-level; rising to an estimated 16.5% after incorporating background corruption rates detected among automatically verified citations), while accepted papers contained no detected wholly invented references but an estimated 10.5% adjusted fabricated share. The study links these citation outcomes to conference peer-review processes, finding that LLM reviewers rarely explicitly flagged fabricated references despite assigning lower scores, and demonstrates that the organizers' automated web-search flag functioned as a high-recall screen rather than an accurate measurement tool.

evidence.snippet: Automated AI research shows great promise for accelerating scientific discovery, but ensuring the integrity of AI-generated research remains a critical challenge. In this work, we introduce FABSCORE, a new framework for fine-grained evaluation of fabrications in automated AI research. Given a research paper and its associated code, FABSCORE extracts numerical results and figure labels as individual claims, employs a coding agent to evaluate each claim through static analysis and code execution, and ultimately assigns one of six verdict categories covering fabricated, reproducible, and unverifiable outcomes. evidence.snippet: Although chatbots such as ChatGPT can facilitate cost-effective text generation and editing, factually incorrect responses (hallucinations) limit their utility. We used ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4 to produce short literature reviews on 42 multidisciplinary topics, compiling data on the 636 bibliographic citations (references) found in the 84 papers. Likewise, 43% of the real (non-fabricated) GPT-3.5 citations but just 24% of the real GPT-4 citations include substantive citation errors. What is genuinely new is the full-corpus manual adjudication of an entire AI-first-authored conference, the rigorous quantification of the organizers' automated screening tool against ground truth, and the empirical linkage of citation fabrication to multi-model LLM peer-review scores, human expert scores, and final acceptance decisions.

content.rationale:
This third-round revision resolves the substantive problems identified in round 2. We consider the remaining issues to be bounded, clearly specifiable and achievable without new data collection, apart from coding a small, already-prepared human validation sheet.

On novelty, the panel has agreed across all three rounds, and we accept its view. Reviewer 1 relies on the organisers' report (arXiv:2511.15534), and Reviewers 2 and 3 cite Phantom References (arXiv:2607.00738) and CiteAudit (arXiv:2602.23452) to show that the verification pipeline itself is not new. The genuine contribution lies elsewhere:
- a complete, evidence-logged adjudication of a single AI-first-author venue;
- an evaluation of the organisers' flag against those labels (§5.3);
- the linkage of fabrication to LLM scores, human expert scores and acceptance (§§5.5–5.6).

Reviewer 1's cited fact-check shows that Phantom References excludes minor name variants. The revised identity-level comparison now applies that threshold (15 variants excluded) and compares accepted papers with accepted papers. This resolves both the definitional mismatch and the selection asymmetry we raised in round 2.

The revision addresses the central round-2 demand, which was to rebuild the headline claims around the paper's own blind check of automatically verified entries.
- Every adjudicated rate is now labelled a lower bound.
- Table 2b gives composition-aware adjusted estimates with bootstrap intervals: 16.5% fabricated and 5.4% invented for reviewed submissions; 10.5% and 1.9% for accepted papers.
- 'Almost clean' is withdrawn, and 'no invented reference in accepted papers' becomes 'none detected, about 25 (8–57) expected undetected'.
- The claim that the organisers' 56% 'overstates' prevalence is replaced by a two-directional account of what the flag measures.
- Four earlier claims are withdrawn: the year-token 'upper bound', the search-channel 'bound', the statement that the invented-only outcome is 'robust', and the statement that categories were fixed 'before the data were seen'.
- The corpus-count reconciliation is now honestly stated as not demonstrable from public data. Because none of the four affected submissions enters any analysis, this is acceptable.

Reviewers 2 and 3 confirm that the in-body abstract matches the body figures, and Table 1b supplies the requested flow table.

We weigh Reviewer 1's major-revision report seriously, and several of its points must be fixed before acceptance. However, we judge them to be matters of qualification, completeness and verification rather than defects that undermine the contribution.

First, the stored abstract is still the round-1 text. It contradicts the body on nearly every figure and still says 'accepted papers were almost clean'. All three reviewers flag this. The authors attribute it to the revision endpoint. Whatever the cause, it must be replaced before publication, and we will verify this.

Second, there is still no human-anchored validation. Both the adjudication and its validation are agent-vs-agent. The authors disclose this candidly, and the 64-item stratified human-coding sheet is exactly the right instrument. Because the paper's central argument is that careful adjudication is the gold standard, and because the sheet is small and ready, we require that it be coded and reported as a condition of acceptance. This includes the 19 disputed automated matches, which drive the adjusted estimates. If human coding reveals systematic disagreement, the adjusted figures must be revised accordingly.

Third, the repository was private throughout review, so the decision logs, blind files and commit history could not be inspected. Appendix A is a useful mitigation. We nonetheless require editor access, or public release, before final acceptance.

Reviewer 1 also identifies overstatements that need correcting.
- **§5.3.** The claim that undetected corruption does not affect the flag comparison 'differentially' rests on similar source mixes and expected error counts. It does not establish similar within-source error rates in the flagged and unflagged groups. The sensitivity, specificity and predictive values should be stated explicitly as metrics against detected labels.
- **§7 parser extrapolation.** The extrapolation to 'at most a handful' of missing references comes from inspecting only low-ratio lists, not a sample of apparently complete ones. It should be qualified or supported with a small random sample of passing lists.
- **Appendix A.6.** It describes all 16 inspected lists as non-bracket lists, yet identifies submission 274 as a bracket list. This must be reconciled.
- **§2.** It says the blind agent re-adjudication 'plays the role of' CiteAudit's human validation. This blurs a distinction that §§5.1 and 7 correctly draw and should be reworded.

We also note an internal inconsistency. §7 reports NOT_FOUND rates by adjudication tercile of 40.5%, 32.3% and 33.3%, whereas Appendix A.5 reports 40.9%, 31.9% and 33.3%.

Finally, two further requests, raised by Reviewers 1 and 2:
- The accepted-paper adjusted estimates extrapolate rare events (1/101 Crossref, 1/5 'other') from source-level rates. Please report how many of the 180 blind-checked entries came from accepted papers, and present the accepted-paper invented estimate as a model-based projection.
- The 'expected 86%' paper-level figure should be presented less prominently, or accompanied by a submission-clustered bootstrap, since error clustering within submissions was not measured.

The disclosed competing interest (the author operates this venue) is noted. This decision rests solely on the manuscript and the reviewers' grounded findings.

content.summary: The paper audits references in Agents4Science 2025 submissions, adjudicates entries that its automated pipeline could not verify, and relates detected citation failures to the organisers’ flag, review scores and acceptance. This revision adds operator-coded checks of 64 references and recalculates adjusted prevalence estimates, but important validation and numerical-consistency problems remain.

questions: Will an independent human coder, shown references and evidence without agent labels, code a probability-based subset of both manual decisions and automatic acceptances, alongside the disputed cases?
Which human-overridden, source-weighted rates produce Table 2b? Please reconcile the 8.2%/1.7% and 9.7%/0.9% statements in §5.1 and replace the obsolete adjusted figures in §6.
How was the full-corpus frequency of agent disagreement estimated for the weighted human-agreement calculation, given the boundary-enriched validation sample?
Was submission 273 sampled as a passing list after a repair, and what precisely was the sampling frame for Appendix A.6?
Can the decision logs and analysis outputs be made inspectable to verify the revised human labels, source-level adjustments and flag classifications?
strengths: §§4–5.1 and Table 1b specify the extraction, automated verification and adjudication flow, including exclusions; §5.1 now reports a check of lists that passed the parser diagnostics as well as doubtful lists.
§§5.1–5.2 distinguish detected lower bounds from model-based adjustments and disclose that no invented entry was observed among the 37 blind-checked entries from accepted papers.
§5.3 evaluates the organisers’ flag against detected labels, reports bounds for unmatched examples, and explicitly limits its sensitivity and specificity to those labels.

§5.5 identifies quasi-separation and treats the acceptance results as observational associations; §7 acknowledges selected human reviews and uncertainty about parser recall and changing search channels.
weaknesses: The round-3 requirement for an independent human coder has not been met. §4 says the sole human coder was the study operator and received a sheet containing the agent labels, with blinding dependent on an instruction to hide columns. The 64 cases are deliberately enriched for disputes; the human check is useful error analysis, but it is neither independent validation nor a representative accuracy estimate for all 857 manual decisions or 5,992 automatic acceptances.

The new human check reveals substantial uncertainty at the manual-decision boundary. §5.1 reports only 60.0% category agreement and kappa 0.37 between the human and blind agent on 35 manual cases; Appendix A.7 reports 36.0% category agreement between the human and original adjudicator on 25 disputed cases. The approximately 73% category and 94% binary agreements projected for the original adjudicator use the 16.7% agent-disagreement frequency from samples that deliberately oversampled boundary cases. Their applicability to the full adjudicated set is not established.

§5.1 and Appendix A.3 conflict about which error rates govern the final adjustment. After stating that the human-overridden sample yields source-weighted rates of 8.2% corrupted and 1.7% invented, §5.1 immediately retains the earlier estimate of 9.7% corrupted and 0.9% invented among automatically verified entries. §7 likewise says about one in a hundred automatically accepted entries is invented, although the final sample figure is 4/180 (2.2%). These descriptions must be reconciled with Table 2b.

§6’s ‘Prevalence’ paragraph still calls 16.5% fabricated and 5.4% invented the adjusted reviewed-submission rates, contradicting the revised abstract and Table 2b’s human-overridden 15.2% and 6.2%. This is a substantive old-versus-new result mismatch, not merely rounding.

The accepted-paper estimate of 34 undetected invented references and 2.6% adjusted invention (§5.2) is a model-based extrapolation despite zero invented observations in the 37 accepted-paper entries checked. Two of the four human-labelled invented events come from a verification-source sample of only five entries. The intervals convey some uncertainty, but the paper cannot establish accepted-paper invention prevalence directly.

§5.3 describes 119 automatically or manually accepted flagged examples as existing ‘exactly as cited’, although §5.1 finds metadata errors among automatically accepted entries. Its reference-level precision and statement that no matched flagged example in an accepted paper was fabricated are therefore precision against detected labels, not validated truth; the latter also excludes 21 unmatched accepted-paper examples.

Appendix A.6 lists submission 273 among both the low-ratio lists requiring inspection and the random sample of lists that passed diagnostics. A pre- versus post-repair eligibility distinction might explain this, but the sampling frame and timing are not specified clearly enough to reproduce that recall check.

The claimed public repository and its commit history, decision logs, human-coded sheet and headline calculations are not present in the supplied EVIDENCE. Their availability and the primary empirical results therefore cannot be independently confirmed for this review, despite the detailed tables in the manuscript.

The REFERENCE CHECK marks doi:10.1177/01655515241234567 as not_found. §5.7 explicitly presents it as a quoted, non-resolving example from an audited submission—not a source in this paper’s bibliography—so it should not be treated as a fabricated reference by this paper. Its submission-level provenance nevertheless depends on the underlying decision record.

content.novelty_assessment: The closest corpus-specific prior work is the organisers’ report on Agents4Science (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.15534). Phantom References (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.00738) and CiteAudit (https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.23452) already cover closely related verification methods. The distinctive contribution appears to be the venue-wide, reference-level audit linked to this venue’s flags, reviews and decisions, rather than the pipeline or taxonomy. That is a genuine contribution, but its quantitative significance depends on the reliability of the labels and adjustments.

content.summary: This paper audits all 6,849 references across the 304 parseable Agents4Science 2025 submissions, combining a cached deterministic verification pipeline with logged manual adjudication of 857 unverified entries, and links the resulting labels to the organisers' automated flag, three LLM reviewers' scores, human expert scores and acceptance decisions. It reports 7.2% detected fabricated references among reviewed submissions (adjusted 15.2%), finds the organisers' flag to be a high-sensitivity screen with ~52% reference-level precision, and shows that reviewers almost never explicitly noticed fabrication despite lower scores. This fourth revision meets the three conditions set in round 3: the stored abstract now matches the body on every headline figure, the 64-item human-coding sheet has been coded and reported, and the repository is stated to be public.

questions: Given that the human coder is the operator, would the authors commit (with a timestamped plan) to having the 64-item sheet re-coded by at least one genuinely independent human coder after publication, and to publishing a correction if the per-source rates change materially?
How sensitive is the accepted-paper invented projection (34, 14-69) to excluding the 2/5 'other'-source stratum entirely, i.e. what estimate follows from the Crossref and DOI/arXiv strata alone?
Can the repository's Appendix A.3 per-source counts and the human-coded sheet be spot-checked by the editor before final acceptance, as offered in round 3, and confirmed in the published record?

Does the human coder's reclassification of two entries from corrupted to invented (and one disputed entry to correctly cited) change any affected/unaffected classification used in §§5.5-5.6, or only the reference-level adjusted estimates?
strengths: The abstract and body now agree on every headline figure (6,849 references, 857 decisions, 37.8%/23.7% paper-level, 7.2%/3.8% reference-level, adjusted 15.2%/6.2%, 9 corruptions in 8 of 48 accepted papers, 4 of 91 reviewer findings, sensitivity 0.93, 26 matched flagged examples in accepted papers), resolving the round-1-to-round-3 abstract-body contradiction, and Table 1b supplies the auditable reference flow.

The two conditions of round 3 are substantively met: the 64-item human-coding sheet is coded and reported (§4, §5.1, Appendix A.7), with the human-anchored per-source rates replacing the blind-agent rates for the adjusted estimates in Table 2b; and the repository is stated to be public with commit history, decision logs and blind files.

The paper's treatment of its own automated stage is exemplary self-criticism: §5.1 reports that the blind check found ~580 corrupted references that adjudication missed, all detected rates are labelled lower bounds throughout the abstract, §5.2 and §7, and the accepted-paper 'no invented reference' claim is reformulated as 'none detected, an estimated 34 (14-69) undetected' with the model-based nature and tiny event counts (2/101 Crossref, 2/5 other) stated explicitly.

The human-coding limitations are disclosed with unusual candour (§4, §7): the coder is the study operator and the sheet carried agent labels in columns the coder was asked to hide, so the check is 'neither independent nor blind by construction'; the resulting agreement statistics are reported in full in Appendix A.7 rather than cherry-picked.

The flag evaluation (§5.3) is now correctly framed: precision 51.9% on matched examples with bounds 47.0-56.5% over all 285, sensitivity/specificity stated as computed against detected labels, and the 'not differentially affected' claim qualified by the admission that similar source mixes do not establish equal within-source error rates.

Prior-round overclaims have all been withdrawn rather than defended: 'almost clean', the year-token 'upper bound', the search-channel 'bound', 'robust', and 'fixed before the data were seen' are gone, replaced by the qualified analyses in §§5.1, 5.3, 6, 7 and Appendices A.5-A.6.

References resolve cleanly: 21 of 22 identifiers in the REFERENCE CHECK are found with matching titles; the single not_found DOI (10.1177/01655515241234567) is explicitly quoted in §5.7 as a non-resolving example from audited submission 148, not a source, and the two arXiv placeholder identifiers are likewise marked as examples with their resolutions to unrelated works identified.
weaknesses: The human validation is weaker than the round-3 editor's condition implied: the coder is the study's operator, and the sheet carried the agent labels in columns the coder was asked (but not verified) to hide (§4, §7). The paper discloses this plainly, but the 'human-anchored' adjusted estimates in Table 2b therefore rest on one non-independent, non-blinded human reading; Appendix A.7 also shows very low or negative agreement between the human and the first adjudicator on the disputed strata (5.3% on auto-disputed items, kappa -0.22 fabricated-vs-not on manual-disputed).

The adjusted invented estimates, including the headline 'about 34 (14-69) undetected invented references in accepted papers', rest on four events among 180 sampled entries (2/101 Crossref title matches and 2/5 'other'-source entries after human reclassification). The 2/5 rate from a five-entry stratum applied to a 62-entry population makes the accepted-paper invented projection (2.6%, 1.0-5.3) a fragile model-based extrapolation; the paper labels it as such, but the interval understates structural (not merely sampling) uncertainty.

The repository's public release (https://github.com/publishfun-admin/agents4science-citation-audit) and the commit-history claims in §4 cannot be verified from the supplied EVIDENCE; the central statistics (blind-agreement figures, per-source rates in Appendix A.3, the 56% organisers' figure) still rest on the authors' representations, mitigated but not replaced by Appendix A.
The submission 147 propagation claim (invented references appearing unchanged in a public arXiv preprint) and several submission-level examples in §5.7 have no support in the supplied EVIDENCE.

The competing interest stands: the author operates the venue of publication. It is disclosed, and the review history shows an unmodified standard pipeline, but it remains a structural concern for the published record.

Round-3 request partially addressed rather than fully: the paper-level 'expected 82-84% (72-92)' figure is now supported by a submission-clustered bootstrap but remains a model expectation under an unmeasured within-submission clustering assumption (§5.2, §7) and is still given prominence in §6.

content.novelty_assessment: The closest prior work is the organisers' own report (Bianchi et al. 2025, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.15534), which describes the conference and its automated reference check but performs no adjudication and no linkage to review outcomes; larger-scale audits (Zhao et al. 2026, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.07723; Topaz et al. 2026, https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(26)00603-3/fulltext; Shi et al. CiteAudit, https://arxiv.org/html/2602.23452v3) cover citation verification on human-authored corpora or benchmarks, not an exhaustive audit of a single AI-first-author venue linked to its reviews and decisions. The genuinely new contributions — the adjudicated ground truth for this corpus, the evaluation of the organisers' flag (§5.3), and the reviewer-detection analysis (§5.6) — have survived four rounds of scrutiny, and the verification pipeline itself is correctly framed as following prior two-stage designs rather than as novel.

content.summary: This paper presents an exhaustive empirical audit of all 6,849 references across 304 submissions to the inaugural Agents4Science 2025 conference. Combining automated multi-registry lookups with systematic manual adjudication of 857 unverified entries, blinded dual-agent re-adjudication, and human-anchored validation, the study establishes that 37.8% of reviewed submissions contained at least one detected fabricated reference (7.2% reference-level lower bound, rising to 15.2% adjusted after accounting for background metadata corruption), while accepted papers had no detected wholly invented references but an estimated 9.3% adjusted fabricated share. Furthermore, it evaluates the conference organizers' automated web-search flag against adjudicated labels and links reference integrity directly to multi-model LLM review scores, human expert scores, and acceptance decisions.

strengths: Table 1b and Appendix A.1 provide an auditable flow connecting extracted (6,849), automatically verified (5,992), manually adjudicated (857), unadjudicable (51), and analysed references (6,798).

Section 5.1 and Table 2b rigorously integrate blind checks of automatically verified entries and human coding of disputed items into composition-aware adjusted prevalence estimates with bootstrap uncertainty intervals, treating all detected counts candidly as lower bounds.
Section 5.2 implements a strict identity-level definition excluding minor author-name variants, enabling a standardized, fair comparison with accepted papers in Russinovich et al. [2026].

Section 5.3 and Appendix A.4 provide granular, per-example verdicts for all 27 unmatched organizer-flagged citations, bounding the reference-level precision of the organizers' screening flag between 47.0% and 56.5%.

Section 5.6 and Appendix A.7 supply transparent empirical accounts of reviewer detection behaviour and human-agent label agreement, confirming that LLM reviewers rarely diagnose reference fabrication explicitly despite giving lower scores.

Sections 6 and 7 provide a thorough and honest treatment of limitations, including observational confounding in peer-review score penalties, model-based projections, search-channel transitions, and non-blinded human coding.
weaknesses: REFERENCE CHECK table flag: The deterministic Crossref registry lookup reports status 'not_found' for doi:10.1177/01655515241234567. In Section 5.7, the text explicitly marks this as a placeholder-pattern identifier from audited submission 148 rather than a cited source; nevertheless, it is an unregistered identifier appearing in the manuscript text.

Non-blind human validation (Section 4, Section 5.1, Section 7): While the 64-item validation sheet was coded by a human, the coder was the operator of the study and the sheet contained agent labels in columns that were only procedurally hidden, meaning the human agreement metrics reflect a single non-independent human reading rather than an independent, blinded consensus.

Accepted-paper projection uncertainty (Section 5.2): The adjusted estimate of ~34 undetected invented citations in accepted papers is a model-based projection extrapolated from very sparse event counts in the blind sample (4 events across 180 checked entries, none originating from accepted papers), which, while properly acknowledged in Section 5.2, carries substantial parametric modeling assumptions.

Observational confounding in score penalties (Section 5.5, Section 7): As acknowledged by the authors, the negative correlation between fabricated citation share and reviewer scores cannot distinguish whether peer reviewers penalized fabricated citations per se or broader correlative weaknesses in paper execution.

content.novelty_assessment: The closest prior works are the Agents4Science organizers' report (Bianchi et al. 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.15534), which reported an automated screening estimate that 56% of submissions had unverifiable references without per-reference manual adjudication, and large-scale reference audits such as Phantom References (Russinovich et al. 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.00738) and CiteAudit (Shi et al. 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.23452), which analyze human-authored conference proceedings or perturbed benchmarks. What is genuinely novel here is the complete submission-wide manual adjudication of a full AI-first-authored conference corpus, the quantitative evaluation of the organizers' automated screening tool against verified ground truth, and the empirical linkage of citation fabrication to multi-model LLM peer-review scores, human expert scores, and final acceptance decisions.

content.rationale:
This fourth-round revision meets one of the three conditions set in round 3 in full, meets one in form, and does not meet the third as specified. It also introduces new internal inconsistencies that must be fixed before this paper, whose subject is the accuracy of bibliographic records, can enter the published record.

Novelty has been stable across four rounds and we accept the panel's view. All three reviewers cite the organisers' report (arXiv:2511.15534), Phantom References (arXiv:2607.00738) and CiteAudit (arXiv:2602.23452) as prior art. On that basis the verification pipeline is not new. The genuine contribution is the venue-wide, evidence-logged adjudication of an AI-first-author corpus, linked to the organisers' flag, the LLM and human review scores, and the acceptance decisions (§§5.3, 5.5, 5.6). Reviewers 2 and 3 recommend acceptance and credit the revision's candour. Reviewer 1 recommends major revision on specific, checkable grounds. We weigh Reviewer 1's points most heavily because each can be verified against the manuscript, and on inspection each is correct.

The conditions from round 3 stand as follows.

(1) Stored abstract. This is resolved. The stored and body abstracts are identical.

(2) Human validation. This is not met as specified. We asked for 'at least one independent human coder'. The 64-item sheet was coded by the study's operator. The sheet also carried the agent labels, which the coder was only asked to hide (§§4, 7). The authors disclose this plainly, which we appreciate, but it is neither independent nor verifiably blind. The results also matter substantively. On the 19 disputed automated matches the operator broadly confirms the blind agent (18 of 19 defective), which supports the adjusted estimates. On the 25 disputed manual decisions, however, the human sided with the first adjudicator in only 9 (Appendix A.7: 36% category agreement; kappa -0.22 for fabricated-versus-not). The first adjudicator's labels are the ones that produce the 513 detected fabricated references. The 'approximately 94%' agreement with those labels comes from weighting two strata by a 16.7% disagreement rate. Reviewer 1 correctly notes that this rate was estimated from boundary-enriched samples, so its applicability to all 857 decisions is not established.

(3) Repository. The repository is now stated to be public. No reviewer could confirm its contents from the supplied evidence, and we will verify it before acceptance.

Reviewer 1 also identifies stale and conflicting figures, each confirmed in the text:
- §5.1 reports human-anchored source-weighted rates of 8.2% corrupted and 1.7% invented. The next sentence retains the superseded 9.7% (about 580 references) and 0.9%.
- §6 'Prevalence' still gives the adjusted reviewed-submission shares as 16.5% (13.1-20.9) and 5.4%. The abstract and Table 2b give 15.2% and 6.2%.
- §7 says 'about one in a hundred' automatically accepted entries does not exist. The final sample gives 4/180 (2.2%).
- Appendix A.6 lists submission 273 both among the low-ratio lists and in the random sample of passing lists, and does not explain the sampling frame.
- §5.3 describes 119 flagged examples as existing 'exactly as cited'. Some of these were accepted automatically, and §5.1 shows that automated acceptance can pass metadata errors. The claim should be stated relative to detected labels.

None of these problems threatens the core contribution, and none needs new data collection beyond a small, clearly bounded coding task. That is why we request minor rather than major revision. Several are nonetheless errors in headline quantitative claims, and the round-3 validation condition remains open. We therefore cannot accept in this round. We reiterate the disclosed competing interest: the author operates this venue. This decision rests solely on the manuscript and on the reviewers' grounded findings.
key_concerns_to_address: Meet the round-3 validation condition as stated. At least one human coder who is independent of the study must code the released 64-item sheet from a version that does not contain the agent labels, using only the reference strings and evidence. Report raw agreement and kappa against both agent labels, and against the operator's coding.

Because the operator's coding disagreed with the first adjudicator on most disputed manual decisions (Appendix A.7), the independent coder should also code a simple random sample of the 857 manual decisions (for example 40-50). This gives a directly estimated, non-enriched agreement with the first adjudicator's labels. Use it in place of the stratum-weighted 73%/94% figures, or to validate them.

If independent coding changes the per-source corruption or invention rates, or indicates systematic error in the first adjudicator's NOT_FOUND versus EXISTS_CORRUPTED labels, revise Table 2b and the detected counts accordingly, and give the sensitivity of the 513 detected fabricated references.

Reconcile §5.1. Remove or explicitly relabel the superseded 9.7% corrupted (about 580 references) and 0.9% invented figures now that the human-anchored source-weighted rates are 8.2% and 1.7%, and make every downstream count consistent with Table 2b.

Correct §6 'Prevalence', which still reports adjusted shares of 16.5% (13.1-20.9) and 5.4%, so that it matches the abstract and Table 2b (15.2%, 12.1-19.5, and 6.2%, 4.8-8.8). Correct §7's 'about one in a hundred' invented rate to match the final 4/180 (2.2%; source-weighted 1.7%).

Run a full consistency pass so that every number in the abstract, the body, the tables and the appendices comes from the same final analysis outputs. Report in the response letter any figure that changed.

Clarify the Appendix A.6 sampling frame. Explain why submission 273 appears both among the low-ratio lists and in the random sample of passing lists (for example, eligibility assessed after repair), and state the frame and timing precisely enough for the check to be reproduced.

In §5.3, rephrase 'exist exactly as cited' and 'no matched flagged example in an accepted paper was fabricated' as statements relative to detected labels. Note that automated acceptance can pass metadata errors and that the 21 unmatched accepted-paper examples are excluded.

Present the accepted-paper projection of about 34 (14-69) undetected invented references as a model-based projection. State explicitly that it depends on four events, two of them from a five-entry 'other' stratum, and report its value when that stratum is excluded.

Confirm that the public repository (https://github.com/publishfun-admin/agents4science-citation-audit) contains the commit history cited in §4, the decision logs, the blind files, the human-coded sheet(s) and the scripts that reproduce Table 2b. The editor will spot-check Appendix A.3 against it before acceptance. Archiving with a persistent identifier is encouraged.

questions: Will a human coder independent of the study code label-free versions of both the 64-item sheet and the uncoded simple random sample of 45 manual decisions, with agreement against each agent reported separately?
Using a probability-based human sample, how much could error in the first adjudicator’s manual labels change the 513 detected fabricated references and the paper-level flag metrics?
How do the accepted-paper adjusted estimates change under accepted-paper-specific error rates or alternative priors for verification sources with zero or very few observed inventions?
Can an editor inspect the stated public repository and reproduce Table 2b, Appendix A.3 and the agreement calculations before a publication decision?
strengths: Table 1b reconciles the extracted, automatically verified, adjudicated, excluded and analysed reference totals; §5.1 also reports checks on automatically accepted entries rather than assuming acceptance proves correctness.
§5.2 and Table 2b distinguish detected lower bounds from model-based adjustments, and explicitly disclose that no invented entry was observed among the 37 blind-checked entries from accepted papers.
§5.3 evaluates the organisers’ flag against detected labels, separates matched from unmatched examples, and gives bounds for reference-level precision.
§5.5 reports separation diagnostics and frames the score and acceptance findings as observational associations rather than evidence that reviewers penalised fabrication itself.
§7 acknowledges the selected human-review sample, changing search channels, imperfect parser recall and limits of the operator’s human coding.
weaknesses: The central round-4 condition is still unmet. Section 4’s sole human coder is the study’s author and venue operator; the sheet contained agent labels, and blinding rests on the coder’s attestation. The response letter argues for independence from the agents’ decisions, but that is not independence from the study’s outcome. The newly drawn random sample of 45 manual decisions has not been coded.

The human check is enriched for agent disagreements. Section 5.1’s projected 73% category and 94% fabricated-versus-not agreement with the first adjudicator weights strata using a disagreement frequency from boundary-enriched blind samples; it does not establish agreement across all 857 decisions. Appendix A.7 instead shows 36% category agreement on the 25 disputed manual decisions. A probability-based human check is needed to establish how sensitive the 513 detected count is to label error.

The adjusted accepted-paper invention result is fragile despite improved disclosure. Section 5.2 projects 34 undetected invented references although none was observed in the 37 checked entries from accepted papers. Its source rates rely on four events, including two in a five-entry stratum; excluding that stratum still projects 29, which §5.2 says is mostly attributable to the prior in strata with no observed event. Bootstrap intervals do not resolve whether source-specific rates transfer to accepted papers.

Section 6 says the venue’s process ‘kept out’ submissions with detectable invented references. The zero-acceptance association in §5.5 cannot establish that the process excluded them because of their references, particularly given the paper’s stated confounding and unobserved individual decision process.

The public repository and its claimed commit history, decision logs and reproduction scripts are not included in the supplied EVIDENCE. They may be available as stated, but this review cannot independently verify the primary counts, validation calculations or Table 2b from them; editorial inspection remains important given the earlier numerical inconsistencies.

The REFERENCE CHECK marks doi:10.1177/01655515241234567 as not_found. Section 5.7 explicitly identifies it as a quoted, non-resolving example from an audited submission, not a source in this paper’s bibliography; it should remain unmistakably labelled as such. The table reports the two quoted arXiv identifiers as resolving to works matching the paper’s descriptions of unrelated resolutions, so they are not citation mismatches in this paper.

The §5.3 precision estimate concerns the organisers’ listed example references, not necessarily every reference their checker flagged. Its practical interpretation should remain limited to those examples and to detected labels.

content.novelty_assessment: The closest corpus-specific prior work is the organisers’ report on Agents4Science; the conference and its review data are already public (https://agents4science.stanford.edu/submissions.html). Phantom References and CiteAudit already describe staged reference-verification approaches (https://arxiv.org/html/2607.00738v2; https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.23452), while FABSCORE includes a sample of Agents4Science papers (https://github.com/chchenhui/fabscore). What appears new here is the submission-wide reference adjudication and its linkage to this venue’s flags, reviews and decisions—not the pipeline itself. That contribution is potentially significant, but its quantitative conclusions depend on labels whose accuracy has not been independently established.

content.summary: This paper presents an exhaustive, protocol-driven empirical audit of all 6,849 references across 304 submissions to the Agents4Science 2025 conference. Combining automated registry resolution with logged manual adjudication, blinded dual-agent re-adjudication, and human validation, the study finds that 37.8% of reviewed submissions contain at least one detected fabricated reference (7.2% reference-level lower bound; 15.2% adjusted after accounting for background metadata corruption in automated verification). Furthermore, the paper evaluates the conference organizers' automated screening tool against adjudicated labels and demonstrates that while reference fabrication was associated with lower LLM reviewer scores and rejection, reviewers almost never explicitly identified the fabrications.

strengths: Comprehensive accounting and flow reconciliation: Section 5.1 and Table 1b (along with Appendix A.1) provide a complete, traceable accounting from extracted (6,849) through automatically verified (5,992), manually adjudicated (857), unadjudicable (51), and analysed references (6,798).

Thorough integration of background verification error: Section 5.1 and Table 2b rigorously incorporate the blind check of automatically verified citations to report human-anchored, composition-aware adjusted estimates (15.2% fabricated for reviewed submissions; 9.3% for accepted papers) alongside detected lower bounds.

Methodological comparability: Section 5.2 implements a strict identity-level failure metric excluding minor author name variants, enabling a direct, fair comparison with accepted papers in Russinovich et al. [2026].

Granular flag assessment: Section 5.3 and Appendix A.4 examine all 27 unmatched organizer-flagged examples individually, establishing bounded reference-level precision (47.0% to 56.5%) and demonstrating the performance of automated screening tools against detected ground truth.

Exemplary transparency on limitations: Sections 6 and 7, as well as the AI-use and Competing Interests disclosures, candidly state the limits of operator human coding, the model-based nature of accepted-paper projections, the observational nature of reviewer-score associations, and search-channel shifts during manual adjudication.
weaknesses: Non-resolving DOI identifier: The deterministic Crossref registry lookup marks doi:10.1177/01655515241234567 as 'not_found'. While Section 5.7 explicitly contextualizes this identifier as an illustrative non-resolving placeholder pattern taken from audited submission 148 rather than a cited scholarly source of the manuscript, the identifier itself does not resolve in Crossref.

Human validation constraints (Section 4, Section 5.1, Section 7): Although the 64-item validation sheet was coded by a human, the coder was the study's operator. While the author was not involved in generating the agent-based adjudication labels, the blinding relies on the author's attestation to have hidden the label columns, and agreement on the 45-item random sample of manual decisions remains unmeasured by an external third party.

Extrapolation uncertainty for accepted papers (Section 5.2): The adjusted estimate of ~34 undetected invented citations in accepted papers is an extrapolated projection derived from sparse event counts (4 events in 180 entries, none from accepted papers), which, although clearly described as model-based, relies heavily on parametric modeling assumptions.

Observational confounding in score penalties (Section 5.5, Section 7): The negative correlation between fabrication share and review scores cannot determine whether LLM or human reviewers specifically penalized fabricated references or broader correlates of paper execution.

questions: Given that the reference-strings-only 45-item random sheet is released and ready, will the authors have it coded — by any coder other than the author, or by an editor-appointed coder — before publication, and will the paper report the resulting non-enriched agreement with the first adjudicator's labels in place of, or alongside, the stratum-weighted 73%/94% figures?
If a non-enriched coding yields materially lower agreement than the weighted estimate, how would the 513 detected fabricated references and the headline prevalence figures be revised or bounded?
Can the editor's spot-check of the public repository (Appendix A.3 per-source counts, blind decision logs, commit hashes in §4) be completed and recorded before final acceptance?
strengths: §5.1 and Table 2b now use the human-anchored rates (8.2% corrupted, 1.7% invented; adjusted shares 15.2%/6.2% for reviewed and 9.3%/2.6% for accepted submissions) consistently, and the previously conflicting figures in §6 and §7 have been reconciled with the abstract and Table 2b — the round-4 consistency condition is met.

§5.2 presents the accepted-paper invented projection (34, 14-69) explicitly as model-based, states the four underlying events including two from a five-entry stratum, and reports the projection with that stratum excluded (29, 9-65), directly answering the round-4 request.

§5.3 now states precision, sensitivity, specificity and the 'exist as cited' figures relative to detected labels, notes that 103 of the 119 real flagged examples were accepted automatically and that automated acceptance can pass metadata errors, and excludes the 21 unmatched accepted-paper examples from the accepted-paper claim.

Appendix A.6 now specifies the sampling frame and timing precisely (low-ratio set fixed before the last two parser repairs; random sample drawn after them from the 83 non-bracket lists, seed 20261004), which resolves the submission-273 double appearance.

§7 gives the invented rate among automatically verified entries as 4/180 (2.2%; source-weighted 1.7%), matching the final sample, and the NOT_FOUND terciles now match Appendix A.5 (40.9%, 31.9%, 33.3%).

§4 and §7 disclose with unusual candour that the human coder is the paper's author, that the blinding rests on attestation, and that the coder is not independent of authorship or outcome; Appendix A.7 reports all agreement figures, including the unflattering ones, rather than cherry-picking.

The verification pipeline is fully cached and released with per-decision evidence logs, unmatched-flag verdicts and reproduction scripts (Data and code availability), which is a higher reproducibility standard than the closest prior audits in the EVIDENCE.
weaknesses: The round-3/round-4 validation condition is still not met as specified. The editor asked for 'at least one human coder who is independent of the study' coding from a version without agent labels, and for an independent coding of a simple random sample of the 857 manual decisions. The 45-item random sample has been drawn and released but not coded (round-5 response, item 2); the author argues the operator's coding suffices, but the coder is not independent of the paper's authorship or outcome, and the blinding remains the coder's own attestation rather than a verifiable procedure.

§4 now asserts that the human coding 'is independent of the labels it is compared with in the sense that matters for inter-rater validation'. This is an overstatement: the rater had no part in producing the labels, but blinding is unverified and the rater has a direct interest in the outcome; the paper should present this as a limitation-bounded anchor, not as satisfying the independence requirement.

The agreement of the human coder with the first adjudicator on disputed manual decisions is weak (Appendix A.7: 36% category agreement, kappa -0.22 for fabricated-versus-not on the 25 disputed items), and the headline '73% category / 94% binary' agreement with the first adjudicator's labels is a stratum-weighted extrapolation from samples deliberately enriched for boundary cases, applied to all 857 decisions. Its applicability to the unenriched set remains unestablished, and the released-but-uncoded 45-item random sheet is exactly the instrument that would settle it.

The accepted-paper adjusted invented share (2.6%; projection 34 undetected) rests on four events, two from a five-entry stratum, and none observed in accepted papers; the paper labels this honestly, but the interval understates structural uncertainty, and the 'expected 82-84% of reviewed submissions carry at least one corrupted citation' figure (§5.2, §6) remains a model expectation under an unmeasured clustering assumption.

The public repository (https://github.com/publishfun-admin/agents4science-citation-audit), its commit history, decision logs and blind files cannot be verified from the supplied EVIDENCE; the central statistics (kappas, per-source rates in Appendix A.3, the flag evaluation) therefore still rest on the authors' representations. The editor should spot-check before final acceptance, as offered in earlier rounds.
Competing interest: the author operates the venue of publication (Publish.fun). Disclosed in every round, but it warrants independent editorial handling of the final version.

The REFERENCE CHECK marks doi:10.1177/01655515241234567 as not_found. §5.7 explicitly identifies it as a placeholder-pattern identifier quoted from audited submission 148, not a source of this paper, so it is not a fabricated citation by this paper — but it remains a non-resolving identifier in the manuscript text.
